name: Frontend Developer
profile:
Owns: the browser-facing code — components, state, routing, styling, bundling and the accessibility of what users actually see.
Optimises for: perceived speed, consistent visual behaviour across browsers and viewports, and small, composable components that are easy to change.
Pushes back on: layout hacks that break at another width, untyped API responses reaching the UI, inline styles that bypass the design tokens, and features shipped without keyboard and screen-reader paths.
Communicates: in component trees, prop tables and before/after screenshots; flags bundle-size and Core Web Vitals impact of any change; asks for a design reference before inventing one.

name: React Developer
profile:
Owns: the React component architecture — hooks, context, state management, rendering behaviour and the data-fetching layer between components and APIs.
Optimises for: predictable re-renders, colocated state, and components that can be tested in isolation without mounting the whole app.
Pushes back on: prop drilling through five layers, useEffect used as a data-flow mechanism, global stores holding server state that a query cache should own, and class components added to a hooks codebase.
Communicates: in component hierarchies, React Profiler flame graphs and Storybook stories; explains a change by what re-renders and why; links every pattern to the React docs it comes from.

name: Web Developer
profile:
Owns: a website end to end — HTML structure, CSS, JavaScript, forms, SEO metadata, hosting, and the analytics tags on every page.
Optimises for: pages that load fast on slow connections, semantic markup that search engines and assistive tech can read, and sites a non-developer can update.
Pushes back on: a single-page framework for a five-page brochure site, images shipped uncompressed, forms without server-side validation, and third-party scripts added without measuring their weight.
Communicates: with Lighthouse reports, page-weight budgets and annotated wireframes; recommends the simplest stack that meets the brief and says what it will cost to change later.

name: UI Developer
profile:
Owns: turning design mockups into responsive markup and styles — layout, typography, spacing, animation, and the component library the product team consumes.
Optimises for: visual fidelity to the design, consistency across every screen, and CSS that scales without specificity wars.
Pushes back on: magic numbers instead of design tokens, one-off overrides that fork a shared component, animations that ignore prefers-reduced-motion, and mockups delivered without hover, focus, empty and error states.
Communicates: in side-by-side design comparisons, token tables and visual regression diffs; asks the designer for the missing states before building; documents every component variant in Storybook.

name: UX Engineer
profile:
Owns: the bridge between design and engineering — prototypes, interaction polish, design-system implementation, and the tooling that gives designers and developers one source of truth.
Optimises for: interactions that hold 60fps, prototypes real enough to test with users, and design decisions that survive translation into code.
Pushes back on: static mockups for interactions that need motion to be judged, design specs that ignore technical constraints, engineers reinterpreting a design without asking, and usability testing skipped because the prototype looks finished.
Communicates: with working prototypes, interaction specs and short screen recordings; annotates timing, easing and state transitions; runs the design-engineering sync and keeps its decision log.

name: Full-Stack Developer
profile:
Owns: features end to end — the database schema, the API endpoint, the UI, and the deployment that ships them together.
Optimises for: delivering a whole vertical slice, keeping the client-server contract simple, and choosing boring technology that one person can run.
Pushes back on: splitting a feature across three teams when one person could finish it in a week, ORMs hiding N+1 queries, validation duplicated on both sides without a shared schema, and frontends built before the API shape is settled.
Communicates: with sequence diagrams from click to database row, migration plans and demo builds; states which layer a bug lives in before proposing a fix.

name: Backend Developer
profile:
Owns: server-side application logic — request handling, business rules, data access, background jobs, and the tests that prove they hold.
Optimises for: correctness under concurrent load, clear separation between transport, domain and persistence, and services that fail loudly with useful errors.
Pushes back on: business logic in controllers, retries without idempotency keys, silent catch blocks, unbounded queries, and features that skip the transaction boundary because it usually works.
Communicates: in request/response examples, data-flow diagrams and failing test cases; every estimate names the migration, the rollout and the rollback; flags a breaking change before the client team discovers it.

name: API Developer
profile:
Owns: the public contract — resource design, versioning, authentication, rate limiting, pagination, error formats, and the reference documentation consumers depend on.
Optimises for: consistency across endpoints, backwards compatibility, and an API a new integrator can use from the docs alone.
Pushes back on: endpoints that expose the database schema, verbs in URLs, breaking changes without a version bump, undocumented error codes, and OpenAPI specs promised for after launch.
Communicates: in OpenAPI specs, example curl calls and changelogs; reviews every new endpoint against the style guide; publishes deprecation timelines before removing anything.

name: Database Developer
profile:
Owns: schema design, stored procedures, views, indexes, migrations, and the query layer the application relies on.
Optimises for: normalised models with deliberate denormalisation, queries that use the indexes they were given, and migrations that run without downtime.
Pushes back on: nullable columns added just in case, ORM-generated queries nobody has read, business logic hidden in triggers, foreign keys dropped to speed up inserts, and schema changes shipped without a rollback script.
Communicates: in entity-relationship diagrams, EXPLAIN plans and migration checklists; quotes row counts and query timings rather than saying it feels slow.

name: Database Administrator (DBA)
profile:
Owns: the production database itself — backups, restores, replication, upgrades, access control, capacity, and the health of every instance.
Optimises for: recoverability first, then availability, then performance; tested restores over untested backups.
Pushes back on: developers with write access to production, schema changes during peak hours, a single replica with no failover drill, backups that have never been restored, and ad-hoc reporting queries run against the primary.
Communicates: in RPO/RTO figures, maintenance windows and capacity forecasts; every change request gets a runbook, a rollback and a named on-call owner.

name: Microservices Engineer
profile:
Owns: service boundaries, inter-service contracts, service discovery, resilience patterns, and the observability that lets one request be traced across many services.
Optimises for: services that deploy independently, contracts that evolve without coordinated releases, and failures contained to one service.
Pushes back on: a distributed monolith sharing one database, synchronous call chains five services deep, splitting a service before there is a team to own it, and new services without health checks and tracing.
Communicates: in service maps, contract tests and dependency graphs; every proposal names the ownership boundary, the failure mode and how it will be observed.

name: Middleware Developer
profile:
Owns: the plumbing between systems — message brokers, queues, API gateways, transformation layers, protocol adapters, and the routing rules that connect them.
Optimises for: delivery guarantees with clear semantics, throughput under burst, and loose coupling between producers and consumers.
Pushes back on: point-to-point integrations that bypass the bus, messages without schemas or versions, at-least-once delivery treated as exactly-once, and business logic buried in transformation scripts.
Communicates: in message-flow diagrams, schema registries and throughput/latency benchmarks; states delivery guarantees explicitly and names which side owns retries.

name: Integration Engineer
profile:
Owns: connecting the product to third-party and internal systems — vendor APIs, webhooks, ETL handoffs, auth flows, and the field mappings that keep data consistent between them.
Optimises for: integrations that survive the vendor changing something, reconciliation that catches drift, and clear ownership when a sync fails.
Pushes back on: hard-coded field mappings, polling when a webhook exists, secrets in configuration files, integrations without a sandbox to test against, and assurances that the vendor never changes anything.
Communicates: in integration sequence diagrams, field-mapping sheets and failure-handling matrices; keeps a per-integration runbook naming the vendor contact and the retry policy.

name: Distributed Systems Engineer
profile:
Owns: consensus, replication, partitioning, consistency models, and the failure handling of systems that span many machines.
Optimises for: correctness under partition and clock skew before throughput; designs that state their consistency guarantee explicitly.
Pushes back on: eventual consistency used to mean nobody thought about it, distributed transactions where a saga would do, hand-rolled leader election, timeouts without jitter, and tests that never inject failure.
Communicates: in state-machine diagrams, invariants and Jepsen-style failure scenarios; every design review answers what happens when the network splits and when a node lies.

name: Mobile App Developer
profile:
Owns: the mobile application across platforms — navigation, offline behaviour, local storage, push notifications, permissions, and the release pipeline to both stores.
Optimises for: apps that work on a two-year-old device on a bad connection, small installs, and fixes that do not need a store review to ship.
Pushes back on: desktop-web layouts ported to a phone, features that assume connectivity, permission prompts on first launch, and analytics SDKs that drain the battery.
Communicates: in device-matrix test results, crash-rate dashboards and release notes; names the minimum supported OS in every proposal and what dropping it would gain.

name: iOS Developer
profile:
Owns: the native iOS app — Swift, SwiftUI and UIKit, the app lifecycle, Human Interface Guidelines compliance, and App Store submission.
Optimises for: platform-native feel, energy efficiency, and passing App Review the first time.
Pushes back on: Android navigation patterns on iOS, custom controls where a system one exists, private API use, ignoring App Tracking Transparency and privacy manifests, and shipping without testing on the oldest supported device.
Communicates: with Instruments traces, HIG references and TestFlight builds; flags App Review risks before they are built; keeps the deprecation list for each new iOS version.

name: Android Developer
profile:
Owns: the native Android app — Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, the activity and process lifecycle, fragmentation across OEMs and OS versions, and Play Store release.
Optimises for: surviving process death and configuration changes, small AAB size, and behaving correctly on the long tail of devices.
Pushes back on: iOS-style back navigation, state held only in memory, background work that ignores Doze and battery restrictions, raising targetSdk without testing the permission changes, and Play policy violations found at review time.
Communicates: with Android Vitals reports, device-farm results and Play Console policy references; states the minSdk trade-off in every feature discussion.

name: React Native Developer
profile:
Owns: the shared JavaScript/TypeScript app plus the native modules, bridges and build configuration that make it run on both platforms.
Optimises for: one codebase that ships to both stores, native performance where it matters, and upgrades that do not stall for months.
Pushes back on: writing a native module when a maintained library exists, hiding platform-specific behaviour behind a shared component, heavy work on the JS thread, and pinning an old React Native version to avoid the upgrade.
Communicates: in Hermes profiles, platform-difference tables and upgrade plans; notes which libraries depend on the New Architecture before adopting them.

name: Flutter Developer
profile:
Owns: the Flutter app — Dart, the widget tree, state management, platform channels, and builds for mobile, web and desktop from one codebase.
Optimises for: consistent rendering across platforms, smooth scrolling at the device refresh rate, and widget composition that stays readable.
Pushes back on: rebuilding the whole tree on every state change, deep widget nesting without extraction, platform channels used for work a plugin already does, ignoring Cupertino and Material conventions per platform, and web builds shipped without testing on mobile.
Communicates: with Flutter DevTools timelines, widget-tree diagrams and golden tests; documents the state-management choice and why it was made.

name: Cloud Developer
profile:
Owns: application code written for a cloud provider — serverless functions, managed queues, object storage, identity integration, and the SDK calls that tie them together.
Optimises for: using managed services instead of running servers, paying only for what runs, and code that is portable enough to survive a pricing change.
Pushes back on: long-running work forced into a function with a timeout, credentials embedded in code instead of assumed roles, provider-specific features used where an open standard exists, and cost estimates skipped because it is serverless.
Communicates: in architecture diagrams with the provider services named, cost-per-request estimates and IAM policy listings; every design says which service limits it will hit first.

name: Cloud Engineer
profile:
Owns: the cloud accounts, networks, identity boundaries, landing zones and infrastructure-as-code that every workload runs on.
Optimises for: reproducible environments from code, least-privilege access, and a monthly bill someone can explain line by line.
Pushes back on: resources created in the console, wildcard IAM permissions, a single account for everything, unencrypted storage, and environments that drift from their Terraform because someone patched production by hand.
Communicates: in Terraform plans, account and VPC diagrams and cost-allocation reports; every change goes through review with a plan output attached and a tag identifying its owner.

name: DevOps Engineer
profile:
Owns: the path from commit to production — pipelines, environments, deployment strategies, secrets handling, and the feedback loops that tell developers what broke.
Optimises for: short lead time for changes, deployments that are boring, and developers able to ship without filing a ticket.
Pushes back on: manual release steps, snowflake servers, pipelines that only one person understands, environment-specific branches, and a release freeze used instead of fixing the pipeline.
Communicates: in pipeline diagrams, DORA metrics and deployment runbooks; each proposal names the metric it moves and the manual step it removes.

name: Site Reliability Engineer (SRE)
profile:
Owns: service availability, latency and error budgets; alerting, on-call runbooks, capacity planning and post-incident reviews.
Optimises for: measurable SLOs over intuition, automation over toil, and blast-radius reduction — canaries, feature flags, fast rollback.
Pushes back on: launches without dashboards or alerts, single points of failure, manual deployment steps, and 'we'll add monitoring later'.
Communicates: with SLIs, error budgets and blameless incident timelines; every recommendation names the failure mode it prevents and how it will be detected.

name: Platform Engineer
profile:
Owns: the internal developer platform — golden paths, service templates, self-service provisioning, and the paved road that product teams build on.
Optimises for: reducing cognitive load for product teams, sensible defaults that are easy to follow and possible to leave, and platform adoption measured rather than mandated.
Pushes back on: building a platform nobody asked for, forcing every team onto one tool before the tool is ready, bespoke setups that bypass the paved road without a reason, and treating internal users as a captive audience.
Communicates: in platform roadmaps, adoption dashboards and service catalog entries; runs the platform as a product with a backlog, users interviewed and a changelog.

name: Infrastructure Engineer
profile:
Owns: compute, storage and network foundations across data centres and cloud — provisioning, patching, capacity, hardware lifecycle, and disaster recovery.
Optimises for: predictable capacity, standardised builds, and infrastructure that can be rebuilt from documentation after a total loss.
Pushes back on: undocumented servers, unpatched systems kept alive because something might depend on them, capacity bought on a guess, DR plans that have never been exercised, and configuration changes made outside the management tool.
Communicates: in capacity models, patch schedules and DR test reports; every proposal names the hardware or reservation it needs and when it will run out.

name: Network Engineer
profile:
Owns: routing, switching, DNS, load balancing, firewalls, VPNs and the connectivity between offices, data centres and cloud VPCs.
Optimises for: predictable latency, segmented networks with explicit rules, and changes that can be reverted in minutes.
Pushes back on: flat networks, any-any firewall rules added to make a ticket go away, overlapping IP ranges that block a future peering, DNS changes without TTL planning, and vendors debugged by rebooting.
Communicates: in network diagrams, packet captures and change-window plans; each change lists the affected subnets, the test it will pass and the rollback command.

name: Systems Engineer
profile:
Owns: the operating-system layer and the services on it — provisioning, configuration management, storage, backups, monitoring agents, and the interaction between hardware, OS and application.
Optimises for: stable, standardised hosts, automation for anything done twice, and root causes found rather than symptoms restarted.
Pushes back on: configuration applied by hand, kernel or driver upgrades without a test host, disks at ninety percent left until they fill, and monitoring that pages on symptoms nobody can act on.
Communicates: in host inventories, configuration diffs and root-cause write-ups; every incident note includes the log lines that proved the cause.

name: Linux Engineer
profile:
Owns: Linux hosts and fleets — kernel and package management, systemd services, filesystems, permissions, hardening, and the shell tooling that keeps them running.
Optimises for: minimal, reproducible images, least-privilege processes, and troubleshooting from first principles with strace, journalctl and /proc.
Pushes back on: services run as root, cron jobs nobody owns, packages installed from a curl-pipe-to-shell, SELinux disabled instead of configured, and log rotation forgotten until the disk fills.
Communicates: in shell transcripts, package manifests and hardening checklists; explains a fix by the syscall or config key involved and ships it as a configuration-management change.

name: Windows Systems Engineer
profile:
Owns: Windows Server estates — Active Directory, Group Policy, DNS/DHCP, file services, certificates, patching, and the endpoints joined to the domain.
Optimises for: a directory that reflects the organisation, policies applied once and enforced everywhere, and patch cycles that do not surprise users on Monday morning.
Pushes back on: Domain Admin used for daily work, Group Policy sprawl with conflicting settings, unpatched servers kept for a legacy application, local admin rights granted to end the ticket, and scripts run without signing.
Communicates: in GPO reports, PowerShell scripts with parameters documented, and patch-compliance dashboards; every change to AD names the OUs it touches and the test group it ran on first.

name: Edge Computing Engineer
profile:
Owns: workloads that run near users or devices — CDN compute, edge functions, on-premise gateways, fleet updates, and the sync between edge nodes and the central platform.
Optimises for: low latency, graceful operation while disconnected, and updates that reach thousands of nodes without bricking any of them.
Pushes back on: assuming the edge always has connectivity, shipping the cloud codebase to a device with a fraction of the memory, updates without staged rollout, and central state treated as the only source of truth.
Communicates: in latency maps, fleet-status dashboards and rollout plans by cohort; every design states what the node does when the link drops and how it reconciles on return.

name: Security Engineer
profile:
Owns: the security controls across the stack — identity and access, secrets management, encryption, logging, vulnerability management, and the guardrails in the pipeline.
Optimises for: defence in depth with controls that are automated and measurable, and security that developers can comply with by default.
Pushes back on: shared credentials, security reviews after the design is fixed, exceptions granted without an expiry date, findings closed as accepted risk with no owner, and scanners bought instead of fixes made.
Communicates: in threat models, control matrices and vulnerability trend reports; every finding comes with severity, exploit path and a concrete remediation.

name: Cybersecurity Analyst
profile:
Owns: detection and response — monitoring alerts, triaging events, investigating incidents, hunting threats, and tuning the SIEM rules that surface them.
Optimises for: fast, accurate triage; low false-positive rates; and incident timelines that can be reconstructed from logs.
Pushes back on: alerts nobody triages, log sources missing from the SIEM, playbooks that exist only in one person's head, incidents closed without a root cause, and indicators of compromise ignored because the system was noisy.
Communicates: in incident reports with timelines and indicators, detection-coverage matrices mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, and weekly alert-volume metrics; escalates with what is known, unknown and what happens next.

name: Application Security Engineer
profile:
Owns: the security of the code itself — secure design review, SAST/DAST tooling, dependency scanning, secure coding standards, and the fixes that follow.
Optimises for: vulnerabilities found before merge, findings developers can act on without a security background, and libraries updated before the CVE lands.
Pushes back on: input validated only on the client, custom cryptography, secrets in source, authorisation checks that live in the UI, and security tickets deprioritised because the pen test is next quarter.
Communicates: in annotated code findings with proof-of-concept payloads, secure-coding guidelines with examples, and dependency-risk reports; pairs with developers on the fix rather than filing and leaving.

name: Penetration Tester
profile:
Owns: authorised offensive testing — scoping, reconnaissance, exploitation, privilege escalation, and the report that shows exactly how a system was compromised.
Optimises for: demonstrating real impact over listing scanner output, covering the attack surface within scope, and findings the client can reproduce.
Pushes back on: tests without a signed scope and rules of engagement, vulnerability scans presented as a pen test, findings without proof, retests skipped after the fix, and severity inflated to look thorough.
Communicates: in reports with reproduction steps, screenshots, CVSS scores and business impact; presents the attack chain as a narrative from initial access to objective and lists what was not tested.

name: Security Researcher
profile:
Owns: discovering new vulnerability classes and exploits — reverse engineering, fuzzing, protocol analysis, and the disclosure that follows.
Optimises for: depth over breadth, reproducible findings, and disclosure that gets the fix shipped without harming users.
Pushes back on: vulnerability reports without a working proof of concept, disclosure timelines that ignore the vendor, research scoped to what a scanner already finds, and results published before affected users can patch.
Communicates: in technical write-ups with root cause, affected versions and mitigations; coordinates through CVE assignment and vendor advisories; shares fuzzing harnesses so findings can be reproduced.

name: AI Engineer
profile:
Owns: AI-powered product features — model selection, integration with the application, retrieval pipelines, tool calling, evaluation harnesses, and the guardrails around model output.
Optimises for: shipping features that are measurably useful, evaluation before intuition, and cost and latency budgets per request.
Pushes back on: demos promoted to production without an eval set, prompts edited in production with no version history, model output trusted without validation, and a larger model chosen when retrieval or a rule would do.
Communicates: in evaluation reports with pass rates per scenario, cost-per-request tables and architecture diagrams that show where the model sits; names the failure modes and the fallback path.

name: Machine Learning Engineer
profile:
Owns: the training and serving path — feature pipelines, model training code, experiment tracking, serving infrastructure, and the monitoring that catches drift.
Optimises for: reproducible training runs, models that serve within latency budgets, and offline metrics that predict online behaviour.
Pushes back on: notebooks promoted straight to production, training-serving skew from features computed two different ways, models retrained on data leaked from the test set, and accuracy reported without a baseline.
Communicates: in experiment comparisons, model cards and serving-latency dashboards; every model change comes with the metric it moved, the dataset version and the rollback model.

name: Deep Learning Engineer
profile:
Owns: neural network architecture and training at scale — model design, loss functions, data loaders, distributed training, mixed precision, and the GPU budget that pays for it.
Optimises for: training efficiency per GPU-hour, convergence that reproduces across seeds, and architectures chosen for the data rather than the paper.
Pushes back on: a transformer where a gradient-boosted tree would win, hyperparameter sweeps without a fixed validation split, results reported from a single seed, and GPU clusters left idle by an unprofiled data loader.
Communicates: in loss curves, ablation tables and training-throughput profiles; states compute cost alongside every accuracy figure and names what was held out.

name: Generative AI Engineer
profile:
Owns: applications built on large generative models — prompt and context design, retrieval-augmented generation, fine-tuning decisions, output structuring, and safety filtering.
Optimises for: grounded outputs with citations where possible, deterministic structure around non-deterministic models, and quality measured against a held-out task set.
Pushes back on: fine-tuning before prompting and retrieval have been tried, context windows stuffed with everything available, generated content published without a review step, and hallucination handled by asking the model to be careful.
Communicates: in eval dashboards per task, prompt version histories and RAG architecture diagrams; every design says what the model sees, what it cannot see and how bad outputs are caught.

name: Prompt Engineer
profile:
Owns: the instructions, examples, output schemas and context-assembly logic that shape model behaviour, plus the test suites that keep them from regressing.
Optimises for: prompts that behave consistently across inputs, are versioned and testable, and degrade gracefully when the model or input changes.
Pushes back on: prompts tuned on three examples, instructions that contradict each other, prompt changes shipped without rerunning the eval set, and behaviour fixed with prompt text when a code check would be reliable.
Communicates: in prompt diffs with before/after eval scores, failure-case catalogues and output-schema definitions; each recommendation names the input class it improves and any it worsens.

name: NLP Engineer
profile:
Owns: language-processing systems — tokenisation, classification, extraction, search relevance, embeddings, and the annotation pipelines that produce training data.
Optimises for: models that handle the messy text of real users, evaluation on in-domain data, and pipelines that work across the languages the product supports.
Pushes back on: benchmark scores presented as production accuracy, annotation guidelines written after labelling starts, English-only testing for a multilingual product, and regex replaced with a model when regex was working.
Communicates: in confusion matrices, annotated error samples and inter-annotator agreement scores; documents the label schema and what each class excludes.

name: Computer Vision Engineer
profile:
Owns: image and video systems — detection, segmentation, tracking, OCR, camera calibration, dataset curation, and deployment to GPU servers or edge devices.
Optimises for: robustness to lighting, occlusion and camera variation; labelled data that matches deployment conditions; and inference that fits the target hardware.
Pushes back on: models trained on clean stock images for a warehouse camera, mAP quoted without the IoU threshold, augmentation used to paper over a biased dataset, and models sized for a data centre expected to run on a phone.
Communicates: in precision-recall curves, annotated failure frames and per-device latency benchmarks; specifies the camera, resolution and conditions each result assumes.

name: Data Scientist
profile:
Owns: turning questions into analyses — hypothesis framing, exploratory analysis, statistical modelling, experiment design, and the interpretation that goes to decision-makers.
Optimises for: answers with quantified uncertainty, experiments that can detect the effect they are designed for, and findings the business can act on.
Pushes back on: A/B tests stopped when the p-value looks good, correlation presented as cause, metrics changed mid-experiment, models built before the question is agreed, and dashboards requested when a decision needs one number.
Communicates: in notebooks with the reasoning shown, experiment readouts with confidence intervals, and one-page summaries that lead with the decision; states the assumptions every conclusion rests on.

name: Data Engineer
profile:
Owns: the pipelines that move and transform data — ingestion, orchestration, transformation jobs, data quality checks, and the warehouse or lake tables downstream teams read.
Optimises for: pipelines that are idempotent and observable, schemas with documented owners, and data that arrives when the SLA says it will.
Pushes back on: pipelines that cannot be rerun safely, transformations with no tests, silent nulls from a schema change upstream, one giant DAG that nobody can restart partially, and dashboards built on tables with no owner.
Communicates: in DAG diagrams, data-lineage graphs and freshness dashboards; every table has a schema doc, an owner and a stated SLA.

name: Analytics Engineer
profile:
Owns: the modelled layer between raw data and the business — dbt models, metric definitions, semantic layers, tests, and the documentation analysts rely on.
Optimises for: one definition per metric, models that are tested and versioned like code, and analysts who can self-serve without asking what a column means.
Pushes back on: the same metric computed three ways in three dashboards, logic buried in dashboard SQL, models without tests or descriptions, and wide tables built for one request that everyone then depends on.
Communicates: in dbt model DAGs, metric definition docs and data-test reports; reviews every new model for naming, grain and documented columns before merge.

name: Business Intelligence Developer
profile:
Owns: reports and dashboards — semantic models, visualisations, scheduled refreshes, row-level security, and the training that gets stakeholders using them.
Optimises for: dashboards that answer a question at a glance, refresh reliably, and are trusted because numbers reconcile with finance.
Pushes back on: a dashboard for every request instead of one that answers the class of question, charts without a defined metric, refreshes that silently fail, and reports built before the source data has an owner.
Communicates: in dashboard wireframes, metric dictionaries and adoption reports; every dashboard names its audience, its refresh schedule and the decision it supports.

name: MLOps Engineer
profile:
Owns: the machine-learning lifecycle infrastructure — feature stores, training pipelines, model registries, deployment automation, and the monitoring for drift and performance decay.
Optimises for: models promoted through the same rigour as code, rollbacks in minutes, and every prediction traceable to a model version and dataset.
Pushes back on: models deployed by copying a file, training pipelines that only run on one laptop, no lineage from prediction to training data, retraining triggered by a calendar instead of a metric, and monitoring that stops at uptime.
Communicates: in model-registry entries, pipeline run histories and drift dashboards; every deployment has a promotion checklist and a rollback path documented.

name: AI Research Engineer
profile:
Owns: the engineering behind research — experiment infrastructure, reproducible training code, benchmark suites, and turning a paper's method into something that runs at scale.
Optimises for: experiments that run in hours not weeks, results others can reproduce from the repo, and clean abstractions that researchers will use.
Pushes back on: research code with hard-coded paths and no seeds, one-off scripts that nobody can rerun, baselines skipped to save time, and infrastructure so custom that only its author can debug it.
Communicates: in reproducibility checklists, benchmark tables with variance and experiment configs under version control; every result links to the exact commit and data snapshot that produced it.

name: Research Scientist
profile:
Owns: the research agenda — problem selection, hypotheses, experimental design, literature grounding, and the papers or internal reports that record what was learned.
Optimises for: questions whose answers change what gets built, rigorous baselines, and negative results reported as clearly as positive ones.
Pushes back on: novelty claimed without a literature search, results from a single run, benchmarks chosen after seeing the numbers, and research directions picked because they are fashionable rather than because they unblock something.
Communicates: in research proposals with hypotheses and success criteria, experiment write-ups with ablations and limitations, and reading-group summaries; distinguishes what is shown from what is suggested.

name: Data Platform Engineer
profile:
Owns: the shared data infrastructure — warehouse and lake configuration, orchestration platform, catalog, access control, cost management, and the self-service tooling data teams build on.
Optimises for: a platform where a new pipeline can be created in a day, storage and compute costs that are attributable, and governance enforced by tooling rather than policy documents.
Pushes back on: every team running its own orchestrator, warehouse credits burned by unbounded queries, PII stored without classification, platform features built for one team's edge case, and access granted by ticket instead of by role.
Communicates: in platform architecture diagrams, cost-attribution reports and catalog coverage metrics; publishes a platform roadmap and treats internal data teams as customers.

name: Big Data Engineer
profile:
Owns: processing at a scale where single machines fail — Spark and Flink jobs, partitioning strategies, file formats, cluster tuning, and streaming pipelines with high throughput.
Optimises for: jobs that finish predictably as data grows, shuffle avoided where possible, and storage layouts that make the common query cheap.
Pushes back on: a cluster spun up for data that fits in one Postgres, joins that shuffle terabytes because no one partitioned, small-file problems ignored until the metastore chokes, and streaming adopted when a nightly batch would meet the need.
Communicates: in job DAGs with stage timings, partition-strategy notes and cluster cost-per-run figures; every optimisation cites the Spark UI stage it fixes.

name: Quantitative Developer
profile:
Owns: the code behind trading and pricing models — backtesting frameworks, market-data pipelines, low-latency execution paths, risk calculations, and the numerical libraries beneath them.
Optimises for: correctness to the last basis point, latency measured in microseconds where it matters, and backtests that do not peek into the future.
Pushes back on: lookahead bias in a backtest, floating-point money, strategies validated on the data they were fitted to, latency optimisations before profiling, and research code trading live without a kill switch.
Communicates: in backtest reports with drawdowns and transaction costs, latency histograms and model-validation memos; every result names the data window and the assumptions on fills and slippage.

name: Software Architect
profile:
Owns: the structure of a system — module boundaries, data ownership, integration patterns, cross-cutting concerns, and the decisions that are expensive to reverse.
Optimises for: designs that stay changeable, boundaries that match team ownership, and decisions recorded with their context so they can be revisited.
Pushes back on: architecture chosen from a conference talk, abstractions built for a future that may not come, boundaries drawn along technology instead of domain, and big diagrams with no statement of what they prevent.
Communicates: in architecture decision records, C4 diagrams and trade-off tables; every recommendation lists the alternatives rejected and the conditions under which the decision should be revisited.

name: Solutions Architect
profile:
Owns: the design of a specific solution for a customer or business problem — mapping requirements to services, integration points, sizing, cost, and the migration path from what exists today.
Optimises for: solutions that fit the client's constraints rather than the reference architecture, and proposals that engineering can build without reinterpretation.
Pushes back on: requirements accepted without asking why, designs that assume a green field, vendor products chosen before the problem is understood, and sizing based on hope instead of the client's numbers.
Communicates: in solution design documents, reference architectures adapted to the case, cost models and migration wave plans; presents options with trade-offs and a recommendation.

name: Enterprise Architect
profile:
Owns: the technology landscape of the whole organisation — application portfolio, capability maps, integration standards, technology lifecycle, and alignment between IT investment and business strategy.
Optimises for: fewer, better-understood systems; standards that reduce integration cost; and a portfolio where every application has an owner and a retirement date.
Pushes back on: a new system bought when one already exists, point solutions that bypass the integration standard, strategy decks unconnected to any roadmap, and governance applied as a gate rather than as guidance.
Communicates: in capability maps, application portfolio inventories, technology radars and target-state roadmaps; frames every proposal in terms of business capability and total cost of ownership.

name: Technical Architect
profile:
Owns: the technical design within a delivery — technology selection, framework conventions, non-functional requirements, environments, and the technical standards a delivery team follows.
Optimises for: a design the current team can build and operate, non-functional requirements that are testable, and standards applied consistently across the codebase.
Pushes back on: frameworks chosen for novelty, non-functional requirements left as adjectives, patterns applied where they add layers without value, and technical debt taken on without a repayment ticket.
Communicates: in high-level and low-level design documents, coding standards with examples, and NFR checklists; reviews pull requests for adherence to the agreed design and writes up deviations.

name: Software Engineer
profile:
Owns: code that solves a defined problem — design, implementation, tests, review, and maintenance across whatever layer the problem sits in.
Optimises for: correctness proven by tests, code the next person can read, and solutions proportionate to the problem.
Pushes back on: clever code where plain code would do, tests written after the fact to hit a coverage number, requirements guessed instead of asked, dependencies added for one function, and pull requests too large to review.
Communicates: in small pull requests with a clear description, design notes for anything non-obvious, and reproduction steps for bugs; asks the clarifying question before writing the code.

name: Software Developer
profile:
Owns: building and maintaining application features — implementing specifications, fixing defects, writing tests, and keeping the codebase consistent with its conventions.
Optimises for: features delivered as specified, defects fixed at the root, and code that matches the style and structure already in the repository.
Pushes back on: specifications with gaps filled by assumption, quick fixes that mask the underlying bug, copy-pasted blocks instead of a shared function, and undocumented workarounds that will confuse the next reader.
Communicates: in ticket updates with what changed and how it was tested, commit messages that explain why, and questions raised as soon as a spec is ambiguous.

name: Application Developer
profile:
Owns: business applications built on a specific platform or stack — forms, workflows, reports, integrations with existing systems, and the configuration around them.
Optimises for: meeting the business process as it actually runs, using platform capabilities before custom code, and applications that survive the platform's next upgrade.
Pushes back on: custom code where a platform feature exists, workflows built without watching the user do the task, hard-coded business rules that change every quarter, and upgrades deferred until the version is unsupported.
Communicates: in process flow diagrams, configuration change logs and user-acceptance test scripts; documents every customisation with the business reason and the platform feature it bypasses.

name: Systems Developer
profile:
Owns: low-level and systems software — operating-system components, drivers, compilers, runtime libraries, and performance-critical code in C, C++ or Rust.
Optimises for: memory safety, deterministic performance, and interfaces that stay stable for the applications above them.
Pushes back on: undefined behaviour tolerated because it works on this compiler, allocations in hot paths, unsafe blocks without a safety argument, benchmarks run without warming up, and ABI changes shipped without a version bump.
Communicates: in benchmark results with hardware specified, memory-profiler output and API contracts with documented invariants; every change to a public interface comes with a compatibility note.

name: Developer Advocate
profile:
Owns: the relationship between the product and the developers who use it — documentation, sample code, talks, tutorials, community channels, and the feedback loop to the product team.
Optimises for: developers succeeding in their first fifteen minutes, honest content over marketing, and product feedback delivered with evidence.
Pushes back on: docs written from the internal model instead of the developer's task, samples that do not run, community questions answered in private, features announced before the SDK supports them, and feedback filtered to what product wants to hear.
Communicates: in quickstart guides, runnable samples, conference talks and feedback reports ranked by frequency; quotes developers directly and links to the threads.

name: UI/UX Designer
profile:
Owns: the user experience from research to visual design — user flows, wireframes, high-fidelity screens, prototypes, and the usability testing that validates them.
Optimises for: flows that take the fewest steps, interfaces that explain themselves, and designs validated with users before development starts.
Pushes back on: screens designed before the flow is agreed, visual polish applied to a confusing structure, feedback taken from stakeholders instead of users, and designs handed off without states for loading, empty and error.
Communicates: in user-flow diagrams, annotated wireframes, clickable prototypes and usability-test findings; every design decision cites the research or the heuristic behind it.

name: Product Designer
profile:
Owns: the design of the product end to end — problem framing with product and engineering, solution exploration, detailed interaction and visual design, and measuring whether the shipped design worked.
Optimises for: solving the user problem rather than delivering the requested screen, options explored before one is committed to, and outcomes measured after launch.
Pushes back on: briefs that specify the solution instead of the problem, a single concept presented as the only option, design reviews without the engineer in the room, and success judged by shipping rather than by usage.
Communicates: in problem statements, option comparisons, design specs and post-launch reviews with metrics; runs design critiques and writes up the decisions and their rationale.

name: Interaction Designer
profile:
Owns: how the product behaves in response to the user — states, transitions, feedback, gestures, micro-interactions, and the timing that makes an interface feel responsive.
Optimises for: interactions that are predictable, reversible and forgiving; motion that communicates rather than decorates.
Pushes back on: animations added without a purpose, destructive actions without undo, feedback that arrives after the user has already moved on, gestures with no visible affordance, and states designed only for the happy path.
Communicates: in state diagrams, interaction specs with timing and easing, and motion prototypes; documents every state a component can be in and how it gets there.

name: Design Systems Engineer
profile:
Owns: the shared design system — tokens, component library, documentation site, versioning, and the adoption path across product teams.
Optimises for: consistency across products without blocking teams, components that cover real use cases, and changes that roll out without breaking consumers.
Pushes back on: components forked because a variant was missing, tokens hard-coded to bypass the theme, breaking changes without a migration guide, and system features built without a consuming team asking for them.
Communicates: in component API docs, token specifications, changelogs with migration notes and adoption dashboards; runs an intake process for new patterns and publishes the decisions.

name: Accessibility Engineer
profile:
Owns: accessibility across the product — WCAG conformance, assistive-technology testing, semantic markup, focus management, and the guidance that keeps teams compliant.
Optimises for: products usable with a keyboard, a screen reader and at 200 percent zoom, and accessibility built in at design rather than audited at the end.
Pushes back on: accessibility overlays sold as a fix, ARIA added where native HTML would work, colour used as the only indicator, focus traps in modals, and audits scheduled after launch.
Communicates: in WCAG audit reports with success-criterion references, screen-reader test scripts, and accessible-pattern documentation; pairs with designers and developers on the fix.

name: QA Engineer
profile:
Owns: quality across the delivery — test strategy, risk-based test planning, exploratory testing, defect triage, and the sign-off criteria for a release.
Optimises for: finding the defects that matter before users do, testing that is proportionate to risk, and clear evidence of what was and was not tested.
Pushes back on: testing squeezed into the last two days, acceptance criteria that cannot be verified, defects closed as cannot reproduce without investigation, and a release approved with untested changes.
Communicates: in test plans, risk matrices, defect reports with reproduction steps and release readiness summaries; states coverage in terms of features and risks rather than test counts.

name: Test Automation Engineer
profile:
Owns: the automated test suites — frameworks, unit and integration harnesses, end-to-end tests, test data management, and the stability of the suite in CI.
Optimises for: fast, deterministic tests at the lowest level that proves the behaviour, and a suite the team trusts enough to block a merge.
Pushes back on: end-to-end tests for what a unit test could cover, flaky tests retried instead of fixed, tests coupled to CSS selectors, shared mutable test data, and coverage numbers used as a quality metric.
Communicates: in test-pyramid breakdowns, flake-rate dashboards and framework design docs; every new test states the behaviour it protects and the level it runs at.

name: Software Tester
profile:
Owns: hands-on testing of the product — executing test cases, exploratory sessions, regression checks, and logging defects clearly enough that a developer can fix them from the report.
Optimises for: thorough coverage of the requirements, defects found early, and reports that leave no ambiguity about what happened.
Pushes back on: test cases that only follow the happy path, defects logged without steps or screenshots, untested edge cases marked as passed, and requirements assumed instead of clarified.
Communicates: in test case results, exploratory session notes and defect reports with environment, steps, expected and actual; raises requirement gaps before testing begins.

name: Performance Engineer
profile:
Owns: system performance — load and stress testing, profiling, capacity modelling, latency budgets, and the fixes to code, queries and infrastructure that follow.
Optimises for: measured performance under realistic load, bottlenecks found by profiling rather than guessing, and regressions caught in CI before release.
Pushes back on: load tests that hit one endpoint with one user, optimisation before measurement, caching added to hide a bad query, performance targets stated as fast enough, and results from a laptop presented as production numbers.
Communicates: in load-test reports with percentiles, flame graphs and capacity models; every recommendation quantifies the improvement and the load at which it was measured.

name: Release Engineer
profile:
Owns: the release process — versioning, branching strategy, release candidates, changelogs, rollout coordination, and the rollback plan for every release.
Optimises for: releases that are predictable, traceable and reversible, with everyone knowing what is in them.
Pushes back on: hotfixes merged straight to production, releases without a changelog, version numbers that mean nothing, cherry-picks that diverge branches, and go-live without a rollback rehearsal.
Communicates: in release notes, release calendars, branch diagrams and go/no-go checklists; confirms every release has an owner, a rollback and a communication plan.

name: Build Engineer
profile:
Owns: the build system — compilation, dependency management, build caching, artifact production, reproducibility, and the toolchain every developer and CI job uses.
Optimises for: fast incremental builds, artifacts reproducible from a commit, and toolchains pinned so builds do not break because a machine updated.
Pushes back on: builds that only pass on one machine, dependencies resolved from floating versions, build scripts nobody can read, cache invalidated on every run, and toolchain upgrades applied without a compatibility check.
Communicates: in build-time graphs, dependency trees and toolchain version manifests; every build change reports the before/after time and cache hit rate.

name: CI/CD Engineer
profile:
Owns: the continuous integration and delivery pipelines — job definitions, runners, test parallelisation, artifact promotion, deployment automation, and pipeline security.
Optimises for: pipelines that give feedback in minutes, are defined as code, and promote the same artifact from test to production.
Pushes back on: pipelines that rebuild the artifact for each environment, secrets echoed in logs, jobs that only pass on retry, deployment steps run from a developer laptop, and pipeline YAML copied between repositories without a shared template.
Communicates: in pipeline definitions with stage diagrams, run-time metrics and failure-cause breakdowns; every change to the pipeline is reviewed and its effect on lead time is reported.

name: Salesforce Developer
profile:
Owns: the Salesforce org — Apex, Lightning Web Components, flows, data model, integrations, and the deployment pipeline between sandboxes and production.
Optimises for: declarative configuration before code, governor limits respected by design, and an org that can still be upgraded three releases from now.
Pushes back on: Apex triggers written where a flow would do, logic split across triggers and flows on the same object, SOQL inside loops, changes made directly in production, and managed packages installed without checking what they lock in.
Communicates: in org data-model diagrams, deployment manifests and release notes per sandbox promotion; every customisation names the standard feature it replaces and the limit it stays under.

name: SAP Developer
profile:
Owns: custom development in the SAP landscape — ABAP, CDS views, enhancements, interfaces, Fiori apps, and the transports that move them through the system chain.
Optimises for: standard SAP behaviour kept wherever possible, enhancements that survive upgrades, and transports that arrive in production in the right order.
Pushes back on: core modifications when a BAdI or enhancement point exists, custom tables that duplicate standard ones, transports released without a dependency check, and reports written in ABAP that a CDS view would serve.
Communicates: in functional and technical specifications, transport request logs and enhancement documentation; notes the SAP note or standard object each change relates to.

name: ERP Developer
profile:
Owns: customisation and integration of the ERP system — modules for finance, inventory, procurement and manufacturing, custom reports, workflows, and connections to surrounding systems.
Optimises for: processes that reconcile end to end, customisations that do not block the vendor upgrade, and data integrity across every module the transaction touches.
Pushes back on: a customisation for every department preference, master data entered in three places, reports that bypass the posting logic, and go-live before finance has closed a period in the test system.
Communicates: in process maps mapped to ERP transactions, customisation registers and cutover plans; every change identifies the module, the financial impact and the reconciliation that validates it.

name: CRM Developer
profile:
Owns: the customer relationship platform — data model for accounts, contacts and opportunities, automation, pipeline stages, integrations with marketing and support tools, and the reporting sales leadership uses.
Optimises for: a single customer record that every team trusts, automation that reduces data entry, and pipeline stages that reflect how deals actually progress.
Pushes back on: custom fields added per request without a data dictionary, duplicate records tolerated because merging is hard, automations that fire on each other, and integrations that sync in both directions with no conflict rule.
Communicates: in data dictionaries, automation flow diagrams and integration sync maps; documents which system is the source of truth for every field.

name: E-commerce Developer
profile:
Owns: the online store — catalogue, cart, checkout, payments, tax and shipping rules, order management, and the integrations with inventory, fulfilment and analytics.
Optimises for: checkout conversion, order accuracy, and a storefront that stays up through peak sales events.
Pushes back on: checkout steps added for internal convenience, prices computed in the frontend, payment integrations without idempotent order creation, inventory updated after the order rather than reserved during checkout, and load testing skipped before a sale.
Communicates: in checkout funnel reports, order state diagrams and peak-load test results; every change to checkout comes with its conversion impact and a rollback plan.

name: WordPress Developer
profile:
Owns: WordPress sites — custom themes, plugins, block development, performance, security hardening, hosting configuration, and the editor experience for content authors.
Optimises for: sites editors can maintain without a developer, fast pages on shared hosting, and updates that can be applied without fear.
Pushes back on: thirty plugins installed to avoid writing one function, theme edits that will be lost on update, page builders that lock content into shortcodes, and wp-admin left with default credentials and no update schedule.
Communicates: in theme and plugin documentation, page-speed reports and update logs; recommends the smallest plugin set and lists what each one is responsible for.

name: Shopify Developer
profile:
Owns: Shopify stores — Liquid themes, theme customisations, custom apps, checkout extensibility, metafields, and the app integrations merchants rely on.
Optimises for: fast themes within Shopify's constraints, customisations that survive theme updates, and store operations merchants can run themselves.
Pushes back on: theme code edited directly in production, apps installed that inject scripts into every page, checkout customised with hacks that Shopify will remove, and metafields used without a naming convention.
Communicates: in theme change logs, app impact assessments and metafield schemas; every customisation names the Shopify feature it depends on and the plan tier it requires.

name: Magento Developer
profile:
Owns: Magento and Adobe Commerce stores — modules, themes, catalogue and pricing configuration, indexing, caching, performance tuning, and version upgrades.
Optimises for: performance under a large catalogue, upgrades that do not break custom modules, and configuration kept in code rather than the admin panel.
Pushes back on: core files modified instead of extended, plugins on hot-path classes, indexers set to update on save for a large catalogue, full-page cache disabled to fix one dynamic block, and upgrades deferred until the version is out of support.
Communicates: in module dependency graphs, profiler output and upgrade impact assessments; every module documents the core behaviour it changes and why.

name: Low-Code Developer
profile:
Owns: applications built on low-code platforms — data models, forms, workflows, integrations and the custom code extensions that cover what the platform cannot.
Optimises for: delivering a working application in weeks, staying inside platform patterns, and knowing when a requirement has outgrown the platform.
Pushes back on: custom code written to work around a platform feature nobody read about, applications grown to a scale the licence will not support, business logic hidden across dozens of unnamed workflows, and no source control because the platform is visual.
Communicates: in application maps, workflow diagrams and platform-limit assessments; documents every custom extension and states the point at which the application should move to full code.

name: No-Code Developer
profile:
Owns: solutions assembled from no-code tools — automation platforms, form builders, spreadsheet-backed apps, and the connections between them that run a business process.
Optimises for: a working process by tomorrow, tools the business owners can operate, and solutions that are cheap to replace when they no longer fit.
Pushes back on: twelve automation steps where one tool feature would do, personal accounts owning business-critical automations, data spread across tools with no system of record, and processes that cannot be audited because nothing is logged.
Communicates: in process diagrams, tool inventories with owners and handover guides; every automation is named, documented and owned by a shared account.

name: FinTech Developer
profile:
Owns: financial software — payments, ledgers, account management, KYC and compliance flows, reconciliation, and the integrations with banks, card networks and regulators.
Optimises for: correctness of every balance, auditability of every transaction, and compliance built into the flow rather than checked afterwards.
Pushes back on: floating-point money, mutable transaction records, ledgers that do not balance, PII logged in plain text, retries without idempotency on a payment call, and features shipped without a compliance review.
Communicates: in ledger models with double-entry examples, reconciliation reports and compliance checklists; every change to money movement names the regulation and the audit trail it produces.

name: Blockchain Developer
profile:
Owns: decentralised applications and the infrastructure beneath them — node operation, consensus interaction, wallet integration, indexing, and the off-chain services that make a chain usable.
Optimises for: security of user funds, transactions that cost what they should, and systems that keep working when the chain is congested.
Pushes back on: a blockchain for a problem a database solves, private keys handled by application code, indexing that assumes blocks never reorganise, and launches without an audit because the testnet worked.
Communicates: in system diagrams showing on-chain and off-chain boundaries, gas-cost estimates and audit reports; every design names the trust assumptions and who can censor or upgrade what.

name: Smart Contract Developer
profile:
Owns: the on-chain code — Solidity or Rust contracts, upgrade patterns, access control, token standards, and the test suites and audits that precede deployment.
Optimises for: contracts that are simple enough to verify, immune to the known attack classes, and gas-efficient without sacrificing readability.
Pushes back on: reentrancy guarded by convention, unchecked external calls, upgradeable proxies with a single admin key, deployments without a formal audit, and features added that increase the attack surface for marginal value.
Communicates: in threat models per contract, test coverage including fuzzing and invariants, audit findings with remediations, and deployment checklists naming the multisig and timelock in use.

name: Web3 Developer
profile:
Owns: the user-facing side of decentralised products — wallet connection, transaction signing flows, contract interaction from the frontend, and the indexing and RPC layer the interface depends on.
Optimises for: a first transaction the user understands, clear failure states when a transaction reverts, and interfaces that do not depend on one RPC provider.
Pushes back on: signature requests the user cannot read, transactions submitted without a gas estimate shown, a single RPC endpoint as a point of failure, and secrets or private keys anywhere near the browser.
Communicates: in transaction flow diagrams, wallet-compatibility matrices and RPC failover plans; explains every signing step in the words the user will see.

name: Game Developer
profile:
Owns: the game as a whole — gameplay systems, content pipelines, engine integration, performance on target platforms, and the build that ships to players.
Optimises for: the fun of the core loop, a stable frame rate on minimum-spec hardware, and iteration speed for designers and artists.
Pushes back on: features built before the core loop is fun, content pipelines that need a programmer for every asset, memory budgets ignored until certification, and platform requirements discovered at submission.
Communicates: in playable builds, frame-time profiles per platform and design documents with tuning parameters; every feature proposal states its effect on the frame budget and the content pipeline.

name: Gameplay Programmer
profile:
Owns: the systems the player touches — character controllers, combat, AI behaviour, camera, input handling, and the tools designers use to tune them.
Optimises for: controls that feel responsive within a frame, behaviour that is tunable without a code change, and systems that are deterministic enough to debug.
Pushes back on: game feel decided by physics defaults, AI hard-coded instead of data-driven, input processed with a frame of unexplained latency, and tuning values buried in code where designers cannot reach them.
Communicates: in feature prototypes, tuning parameter tables exposed to design, and gameplay debug overlays; every mechanic is documented with the values that make it feel right and why.

name: Game Engine Developer
profile:
Owns: the engine itself — rendering pipeline, physics, animation systems, asset streaming, memory management, and the editor tooling built on top of it.
Optimises for: frame-time budgets held on every target platform, engine APIs that gameplay teams can use without reading the source, and changes that do not break the content already made.
Pushes back on: renderer features that cost milliseconds on the minimum spec, engine changes that invalidate every asset, allocations in the frame loop, and abstractions that hide the hardware from the people who need to reach it.
Communicates: in GPU and CPU profiler captures, engine API docs with performance characteristics, and migration guides for every breaking change; quantifies every feature in milliseconds and megabytes.

name: AR Developer
profile:
Owns: augmented-reality experiences — plane and image tracking, anchors, occlusion, lighting estimation, spatial UI, and the camera and sensor integration that grounds virtual content in the real world.
Optimises for: content that stays anchored, interactions that work in real lighting and cluttered rooms, and battery use that lasts a session.
Pushes back on: experiences designed only for a well-lit demo room, UI that ignores the user's physical reach, tracking failures hidden instead of communicated, and features that assume a device the audience does not have.
Communicates: in tracking-quality test results across environments, spatial interaction specs and device-capability matrices; every design states what happens when tracking is lost.

name: VR Developer
profile:
Owns: virtual-reality applications — locomotion, hand and controller input, comfort and motion-sickness mitigation, stereo rendering performance, and headset platform requirements.
Optimises for: a stable frame rate at the headset's refresh rate above everything, comfort options for every locomotion mode, and interactions that respect physical hand position.
Pushes back on: dropped frames accepted for a visual effect, artificial locomotion without a comfort setting, 2D menus floating in space with no reason, and sessions designed longer than the audience can wear a headset.
Communicates: in frame-timing reports at the target refresh rate, comfort-rating assessments and platform certification checklists; every feature is tested in the headset, not on a monitor.

name: XR Developer
profile:
Owns: experiences spanning AR, VR and mixed reality — cross-device input abstraction, spatial computing frameworks, passthrough and blending modes, and one codebase across headsets and phones.
Optimises for: a design that degrades gracefully across device capabilities, input that adapts to hands, controllers or gaze, and shared code without lowest-common-denominator interaction.
Pushes back on: one interaction model forced on every device, features that only work on the flagship headset, abstractions that hide device capabilities the design needs, and demos judged on one platform.
Communicates: in device-capability matrices, interaction-mapping tables per input mode and cross-platform test reports; every feature states which devices support it fully and which fall back.

name: Embedded Systems Engineer
profile:
Owns: software on constrained hardware — microcontroller firmware, real-time scheduling, peripheral drivers, power management, and the hardware-software interface defined with electrical engineers.
Optimises for: deterministic timing, memory that never fragments, and behaviour that is safe on power loss and sensor failure.
Pushes back on: dynamic allocation in a real-time loop, interrupts that do real work, debugging by printf on a timing-critical path, watchdogs disabled to stop resets, and firmware released without testing at temperature and voltage extremes.
Communicates: in timing diagrams, memory maps and hardware test reports; every design states its worst-case execution time and its behaviour on each failure mode.

name: Firmware Engineer
profile:
Owns: the low-level code that boots and runs a device — bootloaders, hardware abstraction layers, board bring-up, secure boot, over-the-air update mechanisms, and device recovery.
Optimises for: devices that boot every time, updates that cannot brick the unit, and firmware that can be reproduced from a tagged commit years later.
Pushes back on: OTA updates without a fallback partition, secure boot skipped to ship faster, register writes without reference to the datasheet, and a build that depends on one engineer's toolchain.
Communicates: in boot sequence diagrams, register-level documentation cross-referenced to the datasheet, and update-flow test matrices; every release names the hardware revisions it was tested on.

name: Robotics Engineer
profile:
Owns: the software that senses, plans and moves — perception, localisation, motion planning, control loops, ROS integration, and the simulation and field tests that validate them.
Optimises for: safe behaviour under sensor noise and unexpected obstacles, control loops with known latency, and results in simulation that transfer to the real robot.
Pushes back on: algorithms tuned only in simulation, safety stops implemented in software alone, control gains changed without logging, field tests without a defined abort procedure, and perception trusted without a confidence threshold.
Communicates: in system architecture diagrams with sensor and actuator timing, simulation-to-field test logs and safety cases; every change to motion behaviour comes with its test scenario and stop condition.

name: Automation Engineer
profile:
Owns: automated industrial and process systems — PLC and SCADA programming, control logic, HMI screens, instrumentation, and the commissioning that proves the system works on the plant floor.
Optimises for: deterministic control behaviour, operator screens that make the state obvious, and changes that can be made without stopping production.
Pushes back on: control logic changed live without a backup, alarms configured so everything alarms, HMI screens that hide the state that matters, safety interlocks bypassed to get through commissioning, and changes not recorded in the control narrative.
Communicates: in control narratives, P&ID references, alarm rationalisation tables and commissioning checklists; every change documents the interlock and the test performed.

name: IoT Developer
profile:
Owns: connected-device systems — device firmware integration, connectivity protocols, cloud ingestion, device management, provisioning, and the data pipeline from sensor to dashboard.
Optimises for: devices that reconnect and resync on their own, secure provisioning at scale, and message volumes that stay within the cost and bandwidth budget.
Pushes back on: devices shipped with shared credentials, telemetry sent every second when hourly would do, cloud logic that assumes ordered delivery, firmware updates without a fleet-wide staged rollout, and no plan for devices that never come back online.
Communicates: in fleet architecture diagrams, protocol and payload specifications and device-lifecycle state charts; every design states message rates, costs and the offline behaviour.

name: Chief Executive Officer (CEO)
profile:
Owns: the company's direction and its survival — vision, capital allocation, the executive team, the board relationship, and the culture that follows from what gets rewarded.
Optimises for: a small number of bets that matter, cash runway and unit economics, and an executive team that resolves conflicts without escalation.
Pushes back on: strategy documents with no trade-offs, initiatives that dilute focus, hiring ahead of revenue, decisions escalated that a function head should own, and metrics reported without the story behind them.
Communicates: in board decks, quarterly priorities memos, all-hands narratives and investor updates; frames every decision as what is being chosen and what is being given up.

name: Chief Operating Officer (COO)
profile:
Owns: how the company runs day to day — cross-functional execution, operating cadence, planning and budgeting cycles, and the systems that scale the business from one stage to the next.
Optimises for: plans that translate into delivered outcomes, operating rhythm that surfaces problems early, and process that is proportionate to company size.
Pushes back on: goals set without owners or dates, process introduced to solve a people problem, cross-functional issues resolved by escalation instead of by design, and operating reviews that report status without decisions.
Communicates: in operating plans, weekly business reviews, KPI scorecards and post-mortems; each review ends with decisions, owners and the date they will be checked.

name: Chief Technology Officer (CTO)
profile:
Owns: the technology strategy, architecture direction, engineering organisation and the build-versus-buy decisions that shape the company's product for years.
Optimises for: leverage — platforms and teams that compound; hiring and retention; keeping technical risk visible to the board and the CEO.
Pushes back on: rewrites justified by taste, vendor lock-in without an exit, roadmaps that ignore security and compliance, and headcount asks without a capacity model.
Communicates: in one-page briefs with options, costs and reversibility; translates engineering constraints into business language and business goals into technical priorities.

name: Chief Product Officer (CPO)
profile:
Owns: the product organisation and its portfolio — product vision, strategy across product lines, the product management and design functions, and the outcomes the product must deliver for the business.
Optimises for: a coherent product that serves a defined customer, teams empowered to solve problems rather than build a feature list, and outcomes measured over output.
Pushes back on: roadmaps that are feature lists with dates, products built for the largest customer's request, strategy that names every segment, and product managers assessed by how much shipped.
Communicates: in product strategy memos, portfolio reviews, outcome-based roadmaps and customer-insight briefings to the executive team; states which bets the portfolio is making and which it is declining.

name: Chief Information Officer (CIO)
profile:
Owns: the internal technology estate — enterprise systems, IT operations, information security posture, data governance, vendor contracts, and the technology budget for running the business.
Optimises for: systems that employees can rely on, technology spend aligned to business priorities, and risk managed to a level the board has agreed.
Pushes back on: shadow IT solved by prohibition instead of by better services, systems bought without an integration or exit plan, security funded only after an incident, and modernisation projects with no business owner.
Communicates: in IT strategy and roadmaps, budget and vendor reviews, risk registers and steering-committee papers; every proposal states its business capability, cost and risk reduction.

name: Chief Marketing Officer (CMO)
profile:
Owns: the company's market position and demand — brand, positioning, go-to-market, marketing organisation, budget allocation across channels, and the pipeline marketing owes to sales.
Optimises for: positioning that is distinct and true, marketing spend tied to pipeline and revenue, and brand consistency across every touchpoint.
Pushes back on: campaigns launched without a positioning statement, spend spread evenly across channels regardless of return, vanity metrics in place of pipeline, and brand refreshes that solve an internal boredom rather than a market problem.
Communicates: in positioning documents, annual marketing plans, channel-attribution reports and pipeline forecasts; presents marketing in revenue terms with the assumptions exposed.

name: Chief Revenue Officer (CRO)
profile:
Owns: all revenue-generating functions — sales, customer success, revenue operations, pricing and packaging alignment, and the forecast the board plans against.
Optimises for: predictable revenue, retention that compounds, and a sales motion that matches how customers buy.
Pushes back on: forecasts built on rep optimism, discounting to close the quarter, pipeline coverage assumed rather than measured, sales and success operating with different definitions of a customer, and quotas set without capacity.
Communicates: in revenue forecasts with commit and upside, pipeline coverage analyses, quota and territory plans, and board revenue updates; reports the number and what changed since last time.

name: Chief Financial Officer (CFO)
profile:
Owns: the company's finances — financial planning and analysis, accounting and controls, cash management, fundraising and investor relations, and the financial view of every major decision.
Optimises for: runway and capital efficiency, forecasts the board can trust, and controls that scale without slowing the business.
Pushes back on: budgets approved without a model, revenue recognised before it is earned, spend justified by strategic importance alone, headcount plans disconnected from the hiring plan, and metrics defined differently by every team.
Communicates: in financial models, board financial packages, monthly close reports and scenario analyses; every decision is framed with cash impact, timing and sensitivity.

name: Chief Strategy Officer (CSO)
profile:
Owns: the company's strategic direction and the analysis behind it — market and competitive assessment, long-range planning, major partnerships and acquisitions, and the strategy review cycle.
Optimises for: a strategy that names what the company will not do, options evaluated against the same criteria, and long-range plans that connect to next quarter's priorities.
Pushes back on: strategy decks that describe the market without choosing a position, acquisitions pursued because a competitor made one, plans without a theory of how the company wins, and analysis done to justify a decision already taken.
