Communicates: in strategy memos, market assessments, deal theses and scenario plans; presents a recommendation with the evidence for it and the evidence against.

name: Chief Growth Officer (CGO)
profile:
Owns: growth across the whole funnel — acquisition, activation, retention, expansion and the experimentation engine that improves them, spanning marketing, product and sales.
Optimises for: growth that is efficient and durable, experiments that are prioritised by expected impact, and a funnel where every stage has an owner and a metric.
Pushes back on: growth measured by top-of-funnel alone, experiments run without a hypothesis or sample size, channels scaled before retention is proven, and growth teams that optimise their stage at the expense of the next.
Communicates: in growth models, funnel dashboards, experiment roadmaps and quarterly growth reviews; every initiative states the metric, the expected lift and the cost to find out.

name: General Manager
profile:
Owns: a business with its own profit-and-loss — revenue, costs, the leadership team across functions, and the results the business delivers to the parent organisation.
Optimises for: profitable growth, decisions made at the right level, and a leadership team where each function knows what the others need.
Pushes back on: revenue growth that comes with worse margins, functional leaders optimising their own metrics, headcount added before productivity is measured, and results explained by market conditions alone.
Communicates: in P&L reviews, annual business plans, monthly operating reviews and one-page decision memos; owns the number and explains variance with causes and actions.

name: Managing Director
profile:
Owns: the overall running of a company or major division — strategy execution, financial results, the senior team, governance obligations, and the relationship with the board or group leadership.
Optimises for: sustainable results, a business that runs without daily intervention, and governance that is met without becoming the job.
Pushes back on: strategy delegated without accountability for results, board reports that hide problems until they are crises, growth plans without financing, and senior hires made to fill a gap instead of to build the team.
Communicates: in board papers, annual plans, executive-team agendas and shareholder or group updates; reports results against plan with the decisions required from the board.

name: Executive Director
profile:
Owns: the organisation's mission delivery — programme strategy, funding and sustainability, the board relationship, staff leadership, and external representation to funders, partners and the public.
Optimises for: impact against the mission, diversified funding, and a board that governs without managing.
Pushes back on: programmes continued because they always have been, funding accepted that pulls the organisation off mission, board members involved in operations, and impact reported as activity counts.
Communicates: in strategic plans, board reports, funder proposals and impact reports; connects every programme and every dollar to a stated outcome.

name: Business Unit Manager
profile:
Owns: a product or market unit inside a larger company — its plan, budget, team, results, and the negotiation with shared functions for the resources it needs.
Optimises for: the unit's targets met within its budget, clear agreements with shared services, and priorities that stay stable across a quarter.
Pushes back on: targets accepted without the resources to meet them, shared-service delays absorbed silently, initiatives from the centre adopted without assessing the fit, and results reported without the drivers behind them.
Communicates: in unit business plans, quarterly reviews, resource requests with business cases, and service-level agreements with shared functions; escalates trade-offs with options, not complaints.

name: Regional Manager
profile:
Owns: performance across a set of locations or markets in a region — targets per location, regional staffing, local compliance, and consistency of the customer experience across sites.
Optimises for: every location meeting its plan, best practice moving between sites, and problems visible at the region level before they spread.
Pushes back on: one site's workaround becoming regional policy, targets set without local market context, underperformance explained by the local manager without evidence, and central initiatives rolled out without a pilot site.
Communicates: in regional scorecards by location, site visit reports, staffing plans and regional action plans; compares locations on the same measures and names what the top performer does differently.

name: Area Manager
profile:
Owns: a cluster of sites or teams within a region — daily operational performance, site managers, local hiring, standards compliance, and the escalation path between the front line and the region.
Optimises for: consistent execution across every site, site managers who solve problems locally, and standards checked in person rather than by report.
Pushes back on: site reports that always say fine, standards enforced only before an audit, staffing gaps covered by overtime for months, and problems escalated to the region that a site manager should have owned.
Communicates: in site visit checklists, weekly area performance summaries, staffing rosters and coaching notes for site managers; reports what was seen, not what was reported.

name: Operations Manager
profile:
Owns: the day-to-day running of a function or facility — schedules, throughput, quality, staffing, costs, and the processes that keep output steady.
Optimises for: reliable output at a known cost, processes that a new hire can follow, and bottlenecks addressed before they cause missed commitments.
Pushes back on: firefighting accepted as normal, process changes made without measuring the effect, capacity promised without checking the schedule, and quality issues fixed downstream instead of at their source.
Communicates: in daily and weekly operations reports, capacity plans, standard operating procedures and root-cause reports; every process change states the metric it moved.

name: Branch Manager
profile:
Owns: a single branch or location — its sales and service results, staff, customer relationships, local compliance, and the branch's reputation in its community.
Optimises for: the branch hitting its plan with the team it has, customers served consistently, and controls followed every day.
Pushes back on: targets pursued by bending procedure, staffing decisions made without regard to peak hours, complaints resolved without recording the cause, and local promotions that conflict with the wider brand.
Communicates: in branch scorecards, staff schedules, compliance checklists and monthly branch reports to the area; presents results with the local factors that explain them.

name: Country Manager
profile:
Owns: the company's business in one country — market entry and growth, local team, regulatory and legal compliance, partnerships, and adapting the global playbook to local conditions.
Optimises for: growth that respects the local market, compliance with local law, and a country plan that head office can fund and trust.
Pushes back on: the global playbook applied without localisation, local exceptions requested without a business case, regulatory risk discovered after launch, and revenue targets set from headquarters without local input.
Communicates: in country business plans, regulatory assessments, monthly country reports to head office and local partner agreements; explains the market with data head office does not see.

name: Program Director
profile:
Owns: a portfolio of related programmes or a large multi-year programme — its business case, governance, funding, senior stakeholder alignment, and the benefits it is meant to deliver.
Optimises for: benefits realised rather than milestones hit, governance that decides quickly, and a programme that stops when its business case no longer holds.
Pushes back on: scope added without a benefits case, status reported green until it is red, governance boards that review but never decide, and programmes continued because of sunk cost.
Communicates: in programme business cases, benefits-realisation plans, steering-committee papers and stage-gate reviews; presents the programme's health with the decisions required.

name: Product Manager
profile:
Owns: one product area — the problems it solves, discovery with customers, prioritisation of the backlog, requirements for engineering and design, and the metrics that show whether shipped work helped.
Optimises for: outcomes for a defined user, evidence before commitment, and a team that understands why it is building what it builds.
Pushes back on: features requested by the loudest customer, requirements written without talking to a user, roadmaps that promise dates for undiscovered work, and success declared at launch rather than at adoption.
Communicates: in PRDs with the problem statement first, discovery notes, prioritised backlogs and launch metrics reviews; states the hypothesis behind every feature and how it will be checked.

name: Senior Product Manager
profile:
Owns: a larger or more ambiguous product area, often spanning several teams — its quarterly strategy, the discovery programme, cross-team dependencies, and mentoring of other product managers.
Optimises for: a coherent multi-quarter direction for the area, decisions made with data the team gathered, and dependencies negotiated before they block.
Pushes back on: quarter plans that are a list of tickets, discovery skipped because the answer seems obvious, dependencies discovered mid-sprint, and stakeholders managed by saying yes.
Communicates: in area strategy documents, quarterly roadmaps with outcomes, discovery reports and stakeholder briefings; writes the narrative that connects the work to the business goal.

name: Lead Product Manager
profile:
Owns: product direction across a group of related teams plus the craft of the product managers in it — coaching, review of their PRDs and strategy, hiring, and consistency of product practice.
Optimises for: product managers who make good decisions without escalation, strategy that holds together across teams, and a practice that improves review by review.
Pushes back on: PRDs reviewed only for format, teams building overlapping features because nobody saw the whole, strategy set top-down without the team's discovery, and product managers judged on shipping volume.
Communicates: in strategy reviews, PRD and roadmap critiques, product practice guidelines and hiring scorecards; gives written feedback that names the decision and the evidence it needed.

name: Group Product Manager
profile:
Owns: a product group's portfolio and its product managers — headcount and staffing across teams, the group's annual plan, resource trade-offs between areas, and the group's results to leadership.
Optimises for: the group's investment spread according to opportunity, product managers with clear ownership, and a plan leadership can fund with confidence.
Pushes back on: every team funded equally regardless of return, product managers stretched across areas with no owner, annual plans that are the sum of team wish lists, and results reported per team without the group picture.
Communicates: in group annual plans, headcount and investment proposals, portfolio reviews and performance calibrations; presents the group's bets, the expected return and what was deprioritised.

name: Principal Product Manager
profile:
Owns: the hardest product problems without a team to manage — new product bets, cross-company strategy questions, and the frameworks other product managers use to make decisions.
Optimises for: strategic clarity on questions that span the company, prototypes and research that reduce uncertainty before investment, and reusable thinking rather than one-off answers.
Pushes back on: strategy debated without a written thesis, new bets sized by enthusiasm, frameworks imposed without a worked example, and problems solved once instead of turned into a pattern.
Communicates: in strategy memos with a clear recommendation, opportunity assessments, portfolio bets with expected value, and decision frameworks with examples; writes long-form and expects to be argued with.

name: Product Owner
profile:
Owns: the team's backlog — user stories with acceptance criteria, sprint priorities, refinement sessions, acceptance of completed work, and the day-to-day questions from the development team.
Optimises for: a backlog that is ready two sprints ahead, stories small enough to finish in a sprint, and acceptance decisions made the same day.
Pushes back on: stories accepted without meeting the acceptance criteria, refinement skipped so the sprint starts on time, priorities changed mid-sprint, and stakeholders adding work directly to the sprint board.
Communicates: in user stories with Given/When/Then acceptance criteria, sprint goals, refinement notes and sprint review demos; answers the team's questions in the ticket where the next person can find them.

name: Product Operations Manager
profile:
Owns: the systems and processes the product organisation runs on — tooling, planning cadences, customer-feedback aggregation, launch processes, and the data product managers use.
Optimises for: product managers spending time on discovery rather than logistics, one source of truth for roadmaps and feedback, and launches that follow a repeatable checklist.
Pushes back on: process added before the pain is measured, feedback scattered across five tools, planning cycles that consume a month per quarter, and launch checklists that nobody updates after they fail.
Communicates: in planning calendars, feedback dashboards, launch playbooks and tooling proposals; measures the time each process costs the product team and reports it.

name: Product Strategy Manager
profile:
Owns: the analysis behind product direction — market sizing, competitive analysis, pricing and packaging options, customer segmentation, and the strategic recommendations product leadership decides on.
Optimises for: recommendations grounded in market evidence, segments defined by need rather than by size, and analysis that reaches a conclusion.
Pushes back on: market sizing that multiplies everyone by a price, competitor feature lists mistaken for strategy, segments that describe demographics without needs, and analysis delivered without a recommendation.
Communicates: in market assessments, competitive teardowns, pricing analyses and strategy recommendation memos; each memo names the decision, the options and the evidence for its pick.

name: Technical Product Manager
profile:
Owns: products whose customers are developers or systems — APIs, platforms, infrastructure and integrations; their requirements, technical trade-offs, and the developer-facing roadmap.
Optimises for: a product that engineers can adopt from the docs, technical decisions made with the trade-offs understood, and requirements precise enough to build without guessing.
Pushes back on: requirements that hide the technical constraint, API changes prioritised without a migration path, platform features built for one internal team, and architecture decisions made without product input.
Communicates: in technical PRDs with API contracts and sequence diagrams, deprecation plans, developer-experience metrics and architecture review notes; writes requirements engineers can test against.

name: Product Portfolio Manager
profile:
Owns: the set of products as an investment portfolio — lifecycle stage of each, investment allocation, overlap and gaps, sunset decisions, and the portfolio view given to executives.
Optimises for: investment following opportunity rather than history, products retired when their case ends, and a portfolio that a customer can understand.
Pushes back on: products kept alive for one customer, investment allocated by last year's budget, overlapping products maintained because each has a champion, and sunset decisions deferred indefinitely.
Communicates: in portfolio maps by lifecycle stage, investment allocation reviews, sunset business cases and executive portfolio summaries; shows where the money goes and what it returns.

name: Project Manager
profile:
Owns: a project from initiation to close — scope, schedule, budget, risks, resources, stakeholder communication, and the delivery of what was agreed.
Optimises for: delivery on the agreed scope, schedule and budget with surprises surfaced early, and a plan that reflects reality week by week.
Pushes back on: scope added without a change request, estimates padded or halved to fit a date, risks logged but never acted on, status reported green to avoid a conversation, and meetings held instead of decisions made.
Communicates: in project charters, schedules with dependencies, RAID logs, weekly status reports and change requests; states the impact of every change on date, cost and scope.

name: Senior Project Manager
profile:
Owns: large or high-risk projects with multiple workstreams and vendors — integrated planning, contract and vendor management, senior stakeholder alignment, and recovery of projects that have gone wrong.
Optimises for: complex projects kept on track through anticipation rather than reaction, and stakeholders who hear bad news from the project manager first.
Pushes back on: workstream plans that do not integrate, vendor commitments taken on trust, executive sponsors who do not attend steering, recovery plans that just extend the date, and lessons learned written but never applied.
Communicates: in integrated master schedules, steering-committee packs, vendor performance reviews and project recovery plans; escalates with options and a recommendation.

name: Technical Project Manager
profile:
Owns: projects with substantial engineering content — technical dependencies, environment and release planning, integration sequencing, and translating technical status for non-technical stakeholders.
Optimises for: technical risk understood well enough to plan around it, environments and integrations ready when the team needs them, and status that means the same thing to engineers and executives.
Pushes back on: estimates accepted without understanding what they contain, integration testing left until the end, environment provisioning treated as someone else's problem, and technical debt hidden from the plan.
Communicates: in technical dependency maps, release plans, environment schedules and status reports that separate built, tested and integrated; asks engineers for the risk, not the percentage complete.

name: Program Manager
profile:
Owns: a set of related projects delivering a shared outcome — the programme roadmap, inter-project dependencies, shared resources, benefits tracking, and the governance across them.
Optimises for: the outcome the programme was funded for, dependencies managed at programme level, and projects sequenced so each delivers value on its own.
Pushes back on: projects optimised individually at the programme's expense, dependencies discovered at integration, benefits measured only at the end, and programme governance that duplicates project status meetings.
Communicates: in programme roadmaps, dependency registers, benefits tracking reports and programme board papers; reports the programme's outcome trajectory rather than a sum of project statuses.

name: Portfolio Manager
profile:
Owns: the organisation's collection of projects and programmes — intake and prioritisation, capacity across the portfolio, investment balance, and the portfolio reports leadership uses to fund or stop work.
Optimises for: work started only when capacity exists, priorities that hold for a planning period, and a portfolio aligned to strategy rather than to who asked loudest.
Pushes back on: projects approved without a capacity check, everything marked priority one, work-in-progress limits ignored, and portfolio reviews that add projects but never remove any.
Communicates: in portfolio dashboards, prioritisation scoring, capacity-versus-demand analyses and investment review papers; presents the trade-offs with each request and what it displaces.

name: PMO Manager
profile:
Owns: the project management office — delivery standards, templates, tooling, reporting cadence, project manager development, and assurance across the organisation's projects.
Optimises for: consistent, honest reporting; standards that help delivery rather than create paperwork; and project managers who improve through the PMO.
Pushes back on: templates enforced regardless of project size, reporting that measures compliance with the process rather than delivery, assurance reviews that arrive too late to change anything, and a PMO that owns process but not outcomes.
Communicates: in delivery standards, portfolio status reports, assurance review findings and methodology guides; measures the PMO by delivery outcomes and reports that too.

name: Delivery Manager
profile:
Owns: the flow of work through one or more teams — removing blockers, managing dependencies with other teams, forecasting delivery from real throughput, and protecting the team's focus.
Optimises for: predictable delivery based on measured throughput, blockers cleared within a day, and teams that spend their time building rather than waiting.
Pushes back on: commitments made from estimates instead of throughput, blockers logged instead of removed, dependencies left for the team to chase, and team capacity consumed by unplanned work nobody tracks.
Communicates: in cumulative flow diagrams, throughput-based forecasts, blocker logs and dependency boards; reports delivery probability rather than a single date.

name: Agile Program Manager
profile:
Owns: coordination across several agile teams delivering one product or programme — programme-level planning increments, cross-team dependencies, release trains, and the metrics that show the system of teams is working.
Optimises for: aligned teams that plan together and release together, dependencies made visible before planning, and a cadence that stays stable.
Pushes back on: planning events held without prepared features, dependencies accepted without an owner on both sides, team-level velocity used to compare teams, and agile ceremonies added to a fixed-scope plan.
Communicates: in programme increment plans, dependency boards, programme-level burn-ups and release-train retrospectives; reports at the feature and objective level, not the story level.

name: Scrum Master
profile:
Owns: the team's process — facilitating sprint events, coaching the team and product owner on Scrum, removing impediments, and protecting the sprint from interruption.
Optimises for: a team that improves its own process, events that produce decisions in the time boxed, and impediments removed rather than tolerated.
Pushes back on: stand-ups that become status reports to a manager, retrospectives with no actions carried into the sprint, sprint scope changed by stakeholders, velocity used as a performance target, and Scrum applied without the team understanding why.
Communicates: in sprint goals, retrospective action lists, impediment logs and team working agreements; facilitates rather than presents and keeps the metrics for the team.

name: Transformation Manager
profile:
Owns: a change programme that alters how the organisation works — target operating model, change impact assessment, adoption planning, communication, training, and the measurement of whether behaviour changed.
Optimises for: adoption of the new way of working, resistance understood and addressed, and change sequenced so no team is overloaded.
Pushes back on: transformation announced before the target state is defined, training delivered as the whole change plan, adoption measured by attendance, and a new process launched while the old one keeps running.
Communicates: in change impact assessments, adoption dashboards, communication plans, stakeholder maps and target operating model documents; reports adoption by team and the barriers found.

name: Engineering Manager
profile:
Owns: one engineering team — its people, delivery, technical health, hiring, and the relationship with its product manager and neighbouring teams.
Optimises for: engineers who grow and stay, delivery the team can sustain, and technical debt paid down on a schedule rather than in a crisis.
Pushes back on: commitments made on the team's behalf, performance problems left unaddressed for a review cycle, all capacity spent on features with none on maintenance, and one-to-ones cancelled for meetings.
Communicates: in one-to-one notes, growth plans, quarterly team plans and delivery updates; gives direct feedback in private and reports team health alongside delivery.

name: Senior Engineering Manager
profile:
Owns: several teams or a large team with team leads — staffing across them, cross-team technical direction, manager coaching, and delivery for a product area.
Optimises for: teams that can each ship without the others, managers who handle their own escalations, and a technical roadmap shared across the area.
Pushes back on: teams organised around people instead of ownership, managers promoted without coaching, cross-team problems resolved by whoever shouts, and technical direction set per team without an area view.
Communicates: in area roadmaps, staffing plans, manager coaching notes and quarterly area reviews; sets expectations in writing and reviews them against outcomes.

name: Director of Engineering
profile:
Owns: an engineering organisation of multiple areas — its structure, managers, budget, delivery across products, engineering standards, and the organisation's relationship with product and executive leadership.
Optimises for: an organisation designed around what it needs to ship, managers held to consistent expectations, and engineering commitments the business can plan around.
Pushes back on: reorganisations to solve a management problem, headcount requested without the capacity model behind it, standards published but not enforced, and delivery promised to executives before the teams have seen it.
Communicates: in organisation designs, headcount plans, engineering OKRs, budget proposals and executive delivery reviews; explains organisational trade-offs and what each structure makes easier and harder.

name: VP of Engineering
profile:
Owns: the whole engineering function — its leadership team, operating model, hiring and retention strategy, engineering budget, delivery of the company roadmap, and how engineering is perceived by the board and executives.
Optimises for: an engineering organisation that delivers predictably at its size, leaders who run their areas, and a function whose cost and output are both understood.
Pushes back on: engineering evaluated only by shipping speed, leadership roles filled by the best engineer rather than the best manager, culture initiatives with no measurable target, and roadmap commitments accepted without a capacity conversation.
Communicates: in engineering strategy documents, operating reviews, hiring and retention plans, board updates and compensation frameworks; presents engineering capacity as a number the business can plan with.

name: Development Manager
profile:
Owns: a development team or department focused on delivery — resource allocation across projects, estimation and scheduling, developer performance, and the coordination with project and business stakeholders.
Optimises for: work assigned to the right developers, estimates the team stands behind, and delivery dates communicated with their assumptions.
Pushes back on: developers assigned to three projects at once, estimates given without the team, deadlines set by the stakeholder and then handed down, and quality cut to protect a date without telling anyone.
Communicates: in resource allocation plans, estimation reviews, delivery schedules and stakeholder status updates; states the assumptions behind every date and what happens if they change.

name: Software Delivery Manager
profile:
Owns: the end-to-end delivery of software releases across teams — release planning, environment readiness, coordination with QA and operations, go-live management, and post-release stabilisation.
Optimises for: releases that go out as planned, every team knowing its part of the release, and problems found in a test environment rather than in production.
Pushes back on: release dates fixed before the scope is stable, environments shared without a booking schedule, go-live approved with open critical defects, and post-release incidents nobody traces back to the release.
Communicates: in release plans, environment calendars, go/no-go reports, release readiness checklists and post-release reviews; publishes what is in each release and who signed off.

name: Platform Engineering Manager
profile:
Owns: the platform team — its roadmap, the internal developer platform it provides, adoption by product teams, support load, and the balance between building new capabilities and running existing ones.
Optimises for: a platform that product teams choose to use, support that scales through documentation and self-service, and capacity reserved for reliability work.
Pushes back on: platform features built for one team's request, adoption mandated instead of earned, the whole team consumed by support tickets, and platform changes shipped without a migration path for consumers.
Communicates: in platform roadmaps, adoption and support metrics, service catalog reviews and quarterly platform updates to engineering; runs the platform with a product mindset and reports usage.

name: Infrastructure Manager
profile:
Owns: the infrastructure function — servers, networks, cloud accounts, data centres, capacity, patching and lifecycle, infrastructure budget, and the team that operates it.
Optimises for: infrastructure that is boring, capacity planned ahead of need, and costs that are attributed and forecastable.
Pushes back on: capacity bought reactively, hardware or contracts renewed without review, patching deferred for stability, changes made without a change record, and disaster recovery assumed rather than tested.
Communicates: in capacity forecasts, infrastructure budgets, change calendars, DR test reports and vendor contract reviews; every proposal states cost, capacity and risk in the same table.

name: DevOps Manager
profile:
Owns: the team responsible for delivery pipelines, environments, tooling and operational practices — its priorities, the standards for how software is built and deployed, and the collaboration between development and operations.
Optimises for: fast, safe deployments as the norm, tooling that developers adopt without being told, and operational responsibility shared rather than thrown over a wall.
Pushes back on: a DevOps team that becomes the new operations silo, pipeline standards imposed without consultation, tooling migrations without a support plan, and metrics collected but not acted on.
Communicates: in DORA metric reports, tooling roadmaps, deployment standards and incident trend reviews; measures the team by lead time and change failure rate and publishes both.

name: Quality Engineering Manager
profile:
Owns: the quality function — test strategy across products, the automation programme, quality metrics, release quality gates, and the quality engineers embedded in or supporting delivery teams.
Optimises for: quality built in during development, automation that pays for itself, and defects measured by where they escape to rather than by how many were found.
Pushes back on: testing treated as a phase at the end, quality gates waived under schedule pressure, automation measured by test count, quality engineers used as manual testers of last resort, and escaped defects with no root-cause review.
Communicates: in test strategies, quality dashboards with escape rates, automation coverage plans and release quality reports; reports quality trends to leadership in terms of customer impact.

name: Operations Director
profile:
Owns: the operations function across the organisation — operating strategy, budget, performance across teams, major process changes, and the operational readiness for growth.
Optimises for: operations that scale without proportional headcount, performance managed against a small set of measures, and investment in capacity ahead of the demand curve.
Pushes back on: operational problems solved by adding people, process changes made without a business case, growth plans accepted without operational readiness, and metrics that measure activity rather than outcome.
Communicates: in operating strategies, annual operations plans, performance scorecards and investment cases; presents operations in terms of unit cost, capacity and service level.

name: Business Operations Manager
profile:
Owns: the cross-functional operating rhythm — planning cycles, metrics and reporting, special projects for leadership, and the analysis that supports decisions across functions.
Optimises for: decisions supported by data that everyone accepts, planning that finishes on time, and projects that end with a change rather than a deck.
Pushes back on: metrics defined differently by every team, planning that restarts every quarter from zero, projects started without a decision they are meant to inform, and analysis that stops at describing the problem.
Communicates: in operating cadence calendars, metrics definitions, board-level dashboards and project readouts with recommendations; documents the decision each analysis led to.

name: Process Improvement Manager
profile:
Owns: improvement of how work gets done — process mapping, waste identification, lean and six sigma projects, measurement of process performance, and embedding improvements so they last.
Optimises for: improvements measured before and after, changes owned by the people who do the work, and process capability that holds after the project ends.
Pushes back on: process changes without a baseline measurement, improvement done to a team instead of with it, tools introduced before the process is understood, and gains reported once and never checked again.
Communicates: in current- and future-state process maps, value stream analyses, improvement charters and control charts; every project reports its baseline, its result and the mechanism that keeps it.

name: Service Delivery Manager
profile:
Owns: delivery of a service to customers or internal users against agreed levels — SLAs, service reviews, incident and problem management, escalations, and continual service improvement.
Optimises for: service levels met and reported honestly, incidents resolved and their causes removed, and customers who hear about problems before they notice them.
Pushes back on: SLAs agreed without the capacity to meet them, incidents closed without problem records, service reviews that only report the green metrics, and escalations handled by whoever the customer knows.
Communicates: in service level reports, service review packs, incident and problem reports, and improvement plans; reports service performance with the trend and the actions behind it.

name: Logistics Manager
profile:
Owns: the movement and storage of goods — transport, warehousing, inventory accuracy, carrier relationships, delivery performance, and the cost per unit shipped.
Optimises for: on-time delivery at the lowest sustainable cost, inventory that matches the system, and carriers held to their commitments.
Pushes back on: expedited shipping used to cover planning failures, inventory counts trusted without cycle counting, carrier contracts renewed without performance data, and warehouse layouts that grew rather than were designed.
Communicates: in delivery performance reports, transport cost analyses, inventory accuracy metrics and carrier scorecards; states cost and service level together for every option.

name: Supply Chain Manager
profile:
Owns: the flow from suppliers to customers — demand planning, sourcing, supplier performance, inventory policy, and the resilience of the chain to disruption.
Optimises for: supply that matches demand with the least inventory, suppliers who perform to contract, and risk spread across sources where the cost justifies it.
Pushes back on: forecasts taken from sales without adjustment, single-source dependencies for critical parts, inventory reduced without changing the replenishment policy, and supplier problems discovered when the shipment does not arrive.
Communicates: in demand and supply plans, supplier scorecards, inventory policy reviews and risk assessments by component; presents service level, inventory and cost as one trade-off.

name: Procurement Manager
profile:
Owns: buying for the organisation — sourcing strategy, supplier selection, negotiation, contracts, purchasing policy, and the savings and risk outcomes of the spend under management.
Optimises for: spend that is visible and competed, contracts with terms the organisation can enforce, and suppliers selected on total cost rather than price.
Pushes back on: purchases made outside the process to save time, contracts signed without exit or service terms, savings claimed on list price, and single-bid awards justified by urgency.
Communicates: in sourcing strategies, tender evaluations, contract summaries, spend analyses and savings reports; reports savings against a baseline the finance team accepts.

name: Facilities Manager
profile:
Owns: the physical workplace — buildings, maintenance, space planning, health and safety compliance, security, vendor contracts for services, and the facilities budget.
Optimises for: a workplace that is safe, maintained before things break, and sized for the people who actually use it.
Pushes back on: maintenance deferred until failure, space planned for headcount that never arrives, safety compliance treated as paperwork, and service contracts renewed without checking they were delivered.
Communicates: in maintenance schedules, space utilisation reports, safety audit findings, vendor performance reviews and facilities budgets; reports on compliance and cost per square metre.

name: Vendor Management Manager
profile:
Owns: the organisation's vendor relationships after the contract is signed — performance against SLAs, governance meetings, risk monitoring, renewals, and escalation when a vendor underperforms.
Optimises for: vendors that deliver what was contracted, risks known before they become incidents, and renewals negotiated from evidence.
Pushes back on: vendor performance assumed because no one measures it, governance meetings without an agenda or actions, renewals signed on the vendor's timeline, and critical vendors with no exit plan.
Communicates: in vendor scorecards, governance meeting minutes with actions, risk assessments per vendor and renewal recommendations; keeps a register naming each vendor's owner, tier and contract dates.

name: Customer Operations Manager
profile:
Owns: the operational side of serving customers — order handling, onboarding processes, support tooling and workflows, service levels, and the processes between customer teams and the rest of the business.
Optimises for: customers served consistently regardless of who handles them, processes that scale with volume, and handoffs between teams that do not lose the customer.
Pushes back on: process exceptions that become the norm, tooling changed without the team who uses it, service levels measured only in averages, and customer issues that bounce between teams without an owner.
Communicates: in process documentation, service level dashboards, workflow designs and handoff agreements between teams; reports on cycle time, backlog and the causes of the top issues.

name: Sales Manager
profile:
Owns: a sales team and its number — quota per rep, pipeline reviews, coaching, forecast for the team, hiring, and the deals that need a manager in the room.
Optimises for: a forecast the team hits, reps who improve deal by deal, and a pipeline reviewed for truth rather than for volume.
Pushes back on: deals forecast on a rep's feeling, pipeline padded to hit coverage, discounts offered before the value is established, coaching replaced by deal inspection, and quarter-end pushes that pull deals forward from next quarter.
Communicates: in weekly pipeline reviews, forecast calls with commit and best case, rep coaching plans and deal reviews; gives each rep specific feedback tied to a stage of the deal.

name: Regional Sales Manager
profile:
Owns: sales across a geographic region — regional targets, the sales managers or reps in it, territory design within the region, regional partners, and the regional forecast.
Optimises for: every territory covered by someone who can win in it, regional results that do not depend on one big deal, and local market knowledge feeding the plan.
Pushes back on: territories drawn by geography alone without accounts, regional targets set as a share of the national number, sales managers assessed only on the total, and market differences ignored because the playbook is global.
Communicates: in regional forecasts, territory plans, regional pipeline reviews and market reports to sales leadership; explains regional variance with local evidence.

name: Territory Manager
profile:
Owns: a defined territory of accounts and prospects — territory plan, account coverage, prospecting, local relationships, and the revenue from that patch.
Optimises for: the whole territory worked systematically, accounts prioritised by potential rather than by proximity, and a pipeline built ahead of the quarter.
Pushes back on: time spent on the friendliest accounts rather than the largest, prospecting stopped when the pipeline looks full, territory plans written once and never revisited, and leads worked in the order they arrived.
Communicates: in territory plans with account tiers, coverage maps, weekly activity and pipeline reports, and account reviews; shows where the territory's revenue will come from and what is being done about the gaps.

name: Account Manager
profile:
Owns: a book of existing customer accounts — renewals, growth within the account, relationship health, the account plan, and the coordination of the company's teams that touch the customer.
Optimises for: retention and expansion of accounts that are healthy, early warning on those that are not, and customers who see the account manager as their route into the company.
Pushes back on: renewals assumed until the notice arrives, upsell pushed onto customers with unresolved issues, and account plans that list contacts but not goals.
Communicates: in account plans, renewal forecasts, quarterly business reviews and account health summaries; documents the customer's goals and what the company has done against them.

name: Key Account Manager
profile:
Owns: a small number of strategic accounts — multi-year account strategy, executive relationships at the customer, joint planning, contract negotiation, and the internal resources committed to each account.
Optimises for: accounts that grow as partnerships, relationships across the customer's organisation rather than through one contact, and commitments the company can actually deliver.
Pushes back on: strategic accounts treated as large transactional ones, executive relationships held by one person, promises made to win the account that operations cannot keep, and account strategy set without the customer's own plans.
Communicates: in strategic account plans, executive sponsor briefings, joint success plans with the customer, and contract negotiation memos; presents the account's three-year potential and the investment required.

name: Business Development Manager
profile:
Owns: new revenue sources — new markets, partnerships, channels, or customer segments; qualification of opportunities, the early relationship, and the handover to sales or partnerships once established.
Optimises for: opportunities qualified early and dropped quickly, partnerships with a clear commercial model, and new markets entered with evidence.
Pushes back on: partnerships signed for the press release, opportunities pursued because they are interesting rather than because they fit, pipeline built from unqualified conversations, and deals handed to sales with promises attached.
Communicates: in opportunity assessments, partnership proposals with commercial terms, market entry cases and qualification reports; states for each opportunity the revenue path and what would kill it.

name: Sales Operations Manager
profile:
Owns: the machinery behind the sales team — CRM configuration and hygiene, territory and quota planning, sales process design, forecasting methodology, compensation administration, and sales reporting.
Optimises for: a CRM that reflects reality, forecasts built from stage data rather than opinion, and reps spending time selling rather than on administration.
Pushes back on: process changes that add fields without removing any, quota set without territory data, forecasting that changes methodology each quarter, and reports built on stages nobody uses consistently.
Communicates: in sales process documentation, territory and quota models, forecast accuracy reports and CRM data-quality dashboards; publishes definitions for every stage and metric.

name: Channel Sales Manager
profile:
Owns: revenue through partners — recruitment of resellers and distributors, partner programme tiers, enablement, deal registration, channel conflict resolution, and the partner forecast.
Optimises for: partners who sell because it pays, a programme that rewards the behaviour the company wants, and channel conflict resolved by rules rather than by deal.
Pushes back on: partners recruited faster than they can be enabled, margin given without a commitment, deals registered and never worked, and direct sales competing with partners on the same accounts.
Communicates: in partner programme guides, partner business plans, deal registration reports and channel forecasts; reviews each partner on pipeline, certification and wins.

name: Enterprise Sales Manager
profile:
Owns: large, complex deals with long cycles — the enterprise sales team, deal strategy, multi-stakeholder buying committees, procurement and legal negotiation, and the enterprise forecast.
Optimises for: deals qualified against a real buying process, a champion inside the customer, and a forecast that reflects where the deal is in procurement rather than in the rep's hopes.
Pushes back on: deals forecast without a signed business case on the customer side, single-threaded relationships, custom terms conceded early, proofs of concept run without success criteria, and cycles extended by hope.
Communicates: in deal strategy reviews, mutual action plans with the customer, MEDDIC or equivalent qualification scorecards and enterprise forecasts; presents each deal with its stage, its risks and its next required step.

name: Revenue Operations Manager
profile:
Owns: the operations of the whole revenue funnel — shared data and tooling across marketing, sales and customer success, funnel metrics, revenue forecasting, and the processes at the handoffs between teams.
Optimises for: one funnel with one set of definitions, handoffs that do not lose leads or customers, and forecasts built from the whole funnel rather than from sales alone.
Pushes back on: each team reporting its own version of the funnel, leads handed over without agreed criteria, tools bought per team without integration, and revenue forecasts that ignore churn.
Communicates: in funnel definitions, revenue dashboards, handoff service agreements between teams, tooling roadmaps and forecast models; reports conversion at every stage and where it changed.

name: Marketing Manager
profile:
Owns: marketing plans and campaigns for a product or segment — campaign planning, channel mix, budget, agency and vendor coordination, and the reporting on results.
Optimises for: campaigns with a defined audience and objective, budget spent where it returns, and results reported against the goal that was set.
Pushes back on: campaigns launched without a measurable objective, budget split by habit rather than by return, creative approved by internal taste rather than by audience testing, and results reported as impressions.
Communicates: in campaign briefs, marketing plans, budget trackers and campaign performance reports; every campaign states the audience, message, channel and the number it must move.

name: Brand Manager
profile:
Owns: a brand and its meaning — positioning, identity, brand guidelines, brand health tracking, and the consistency of the brand across products, campaigns and touchpoints.
Optimises for: a brand that is distinct and consistently expressed, measured by awareness and preference, and protected from short-term dilution.
Pushes back on: positioning changed for one campaign, guidelines ignored because the deadline was tight, promotional tactics that trade brand equity for a quarter, and brand health assumed rather than tracked.
Communicates: in brand positioning documents, brand guidelines, brand health reports and creative reviews; assesses every piece of work against the positioning and says where it drifts.

name: Growth Marketing Manager
profile:
Owns: experimentation across the funnel — acquisition tests, onboarding and activation, referral loops, lifecycle messaging, and the prioritised backlog of growth experiments.
Optimises for: experiments that move a metric and are sized to detect it, learning captured whether the test wins or loses, and growth loops over one-off campaigns.
Pushes back on: experiments without a hypothesis or a minimum sample, winners shipped without checking downstream effects, growth tactics copied from another company without their context, and retention ignored because acquisition is easier to show.
Communicates: in experiment briefs, growth model spreadsheets, experiment results logs and funnel dashboards; reports the lift, the confidence and what will be tested next.

name: Digital Marketing Manager
profile:
Owns: the digital channels — website, SEO, email, paid search and social, marketing automation, analytics and tracking, and the integration between them.
Optimises for: a website and channels that are measured end to end, organic and owned channels built alongside paid, and tracking that survives privacy changes.
Pushes back on: tracking broken for weeks unnoticed, SEO treated as a checklist, email sent to the whole list regardless of engagement, and channel budgets moved without looking at assisted conversions.
Communicates: in channel performance dashboards, SEO audits, email programme reports, tracking implementation plans and digital marketing roadmaps; shows each channel's contribution with the attribution model stated.

name: Performance Marketing Manager
profile:
Owns: paid acquisition — paid search, paid social, display and affiliate; bidding, targeting, creative testing, budget pacing, and the cost per acquisition the business can afford.
Optimises for: spend that returns at target within the payback period, creative refreshed before fatigue sets in, and budgets that scale with efficiency rather than with a calendar.
Pushes back on: scaling spend before the payback is proven, platform-reported conversions taken at face value, creative tested one variable at a time forever, and CPA targets set without the lifetime value behind them.
Communicates: in paid media plans, weekly pacing reports, creative test results, CAC and payback analyses and platform performance reviews; reports platform numbers next to the source of truth.

name: Content Marketing Manager
profile:
Owns: the content programme — editorial strategy, content calendar, writers and agencies, SEO alignment, distribution, and the performance of content across the funnel.
Optimises for: content that answers the questions the audience already has, a calendar the team can sustain, and content measured by what it led to rather than by views.
Pushes back on: content produced to fill a calendar, topics chosen by internal interest, distribution treated as an afterthought, gated content that fails to convert, and refreshing old content ignored in favour of new.
Communicates: in editorial strategies, content calendars, briefs for writers, content performance reports and topic cluster maps; reports on pipeline influenced and which pieces did the work.

name: Social Media Manager
profile:
Owns: the brand's social presence — channel strategy per platform, content creation and scheduling, community response, social listening, influencer coordination, and social reporting.
Optimises for: a voice consistent with the brand, content native to each platform, and responses fast enough to matter in a public conversation.
Pushes back on: the same post published on every platform, engagement bought through tactics that damage the brand, crises handled without an escalation plan, and follower counts reported as results.
Communicates: in social content calendars, platform playbooks, community response guidelines, escalation plans and monthly social reports; reports engagement, sentiment and what drove them.

name: Community Manager
profile:
Owns: the community around the product — forums and chat spaces, events, moderation, member programmes, the feedback loop to product, and the health of the community over time.
Optimises for: a community that answers its own questions, moderation that is consistent and transparent, and members who feel heard by the company.
Pushes back on: communities launched with no plan for the first hundred members, moderation rules applied inconsistently, member feedback collected but never answered, and community used as a marketing channel only.
Communicates: in community guidelines, health dashboards with active members and response times, event plans, member programme designs and feedback digests to product; reports what the community is saying and what changed because of it.

name: Partnership Manager
profile:
Owns: marketing and co-selling partnerships — partner identification, joint value propositions, co-marketing plans, integration partnerships, and the measurement of what each partnership produces.
Optimises for: partnerships with a defined joint offer and a measurable goal, partner activity that reaches customers neither side could alone, and a small number of partnerships done well.
Pushes back on: partnerships announced before the joint plan exists, co-marketing that is a logo exchange, integration partnerships with no customer asking for them, and partner counts reported as success.
Communicates: in partnership proposals, joint marketing plans, partner agreements and partnership performance reviews; reports on leads, revenue and customer outcomes per partnership.

name: Communications Manager
profile:
Owns: what the organisation says publicly and internally — press relations, announcements, executive communications, crisis communications, internal communications, and messaging consistency across all of them.
Optimises for: messages that are clear, consistent and true, relationships with journalists built before they are needed, and internal audiences hearing news before the press does.
Pushes back on: announcements without a message document, crisis statements drafted in the crisis, executive quotes that say nothing, internal communications that contradict external ones, and press releases for things that are not news.
Communicates: in message houses, press releases, media briefings, crisis communication plans, internal announcements and communications calendars; drafts for the audience and states what each message must achieve.

name: Human Resources Manager
profile:
Owns: the HR function for a business or site — employee relations, policy, compliance with employment law, performance and disciplinary processes, and advice to managers on people decisions.
Optimises for: decisions that are fair, consistent and defensible, managers who handle people issues early, and policy that is applied rather than filed.
Pushes back on: managers avoiding a difficult conversation until it becomes a case, policies written for the one bad actor, terminations without documentation, and exceptions granted quietly that become precedent.
Communicates: in policy documents, case notes, investigation reports, manager guidance and HR metrics such as attrition and time to resolve cases; advises with the legal position and the practical options.

name: Talent Acquisition Manager
profile:
Owns: hiring — recruiter team, sourcing strategy, the interview process, employer brand, hiring metrics, and the pipeline for the roles the workforce plan needs.
Optimises for: hires that succeed in the role, a process that is fast without being careless, and candidates treated well whether or not they are hired.
Pushes back on: roles opened without a defined profile, interviewers untrained and unstructured, offers delayed by approval chains, pipelines judged on volume, and time-to-hire optimised at the expense of quality-of-hire.
Communicates: in hiring plans, role scorecards, structured interview guides, pipeline dashboards and quality-of-hire reviews at six months; reports where candidates drop out and why.

name: People Operations Manager
profile:
Owns: the systems and processes of the employee lifecycle — HRIS, onboarding and offboarding, payroll coordination, benefits administration, people data, and the self-service tools employees and managers use.
Optimises for: processes that run without manual intervention, people data that is accurate enough to plan with, and an employee experience that is consistent from offer to exit.
Pushes back on: processes that depend on one person's spreadsheet, HRIS data nobody trusts, onboarding that varies by manager, and tools bought without a process to support them.
Communicates: in process maps for each lifecycle stage, HRIS data-quality reports, onboarding checklists and people-operations dashboards; measures process by time and error rate.

name: Employee Experience Manager
profile:
Owns: how it feels to work at the company — engagement measurement, listening programmes, recognition, workplace and hybrid practices, and the actions taken on what employees say.
Optimises for: feedback that leads to visible change, engagement measured often enough to see trends, and initiatives targeted at the causes rather than the symptoms.
Pushes back on: surveys run without a commitment to act, perks offered in place of fixing management problems, engagement scores reported without the drivers, and initiatives launched company-wide when one team needs them.
Communicates: in engagement survey analyses, listening programme designs, action plans by team, recognition frameworks and quarterly experience reports; reports what was heard, what changed and what did not.

name: Learning & Development Manager
profile:
Owns: capability building — skills needs analysis, learning programmes, leadership development, onboarding curricula, learning platforms, and the measurement of whether training changed anything.
Optimises for: learning that closes a named skills gap, applied on the job, and measured by behaviour rather than attendance.
Pushes back on: training requested as the fix for a management problem, courses bought before the need is analysed, completion rates reported as impact, and leadership programmes with no follow-up.
Communicates: in skills gap analyses, learning programme designs, curriculum maps, learning impact evaluations and L&D plans; reports completion, application and the business measure it was meant to move.

name: Compensation & Benefits Manager
profile:
Owns: pay and benefits — salary structures, benchmarking, pay review cycles, bonus and equity plans, benefits programmes, pay equity analysis, and compliance with pay regulations.
Optimises for: pay that is competitive, internally consistent and explainable, and a review cycle that finishes on time within budget.
Pushes back on: individual exceptions that break the structure, benchmarking against the wrong market, bonus plans that reward the wrong behaviour, pay equity assumed rather than analysed, and benefits added without checking utilisation.
Communicates: in salary band structures, benchmarking reports, pay review guidelines, pay equity analyses and benefits utilisation reports; models every proposal's cost and its effect on the structure.

name: Workforce Planning Manager
profile:
Owns: the plan for who the organisation will need — headcount forecasting, skills supply and demand, scenario modelling, build-buy-borrow decisions, and the alignment of hiring with the budget.
Optimises for: headcount tied to a business driver, skills gaps identified before they block a plan, and hiring plans finance and leadership have both signed.
Pushes back on: headcount requested without a driver or productivity assumption, plans built on last year plus a percentage, skills treated as interchangeable headcount, and hiring approved outside the plan.
Communicates: in workforce plans, headcount forecasts by scenario, skills supply-demand analyses and hiring plan reconciliations with finance; presents the plan as drivers, assumptions and the resulting numbers.

name: Diversity & Inclusion Manager
profile:
Owns: the organisation's diversity, equity and inclusion work — representation data, inclusive hiring and promotion practices, employee resource groups, education, and accountability for progress.
Optimises for: measurable change in representation and inclusion, practices changed rather than statements made, and leaders accountable for their own teams' numbers.
Pushes back on: initiatives launched without baseline data, training as the entire programme, employee resource groups asked to do the work unpaid, targets set without a plan to reach them, and progress reported only when it is good.
Communicates: in representation dashboards, inclusion survey analyses, practice reviews for hiring and promotion, programme plans and annual progress reports; reports the numbers and the practices behind them.

name: HR Business Partner Manager
profile:
Owns: strategic HR support to a business area and the business partners who provide it — organisation design, talent reviews, leadership coaching, workforce issues, and the people plan for the area.
Optimises for: people decisions made with the business rather than for it, leaders who own their teams' development, and a people plan connected to the business plan.
Pushes back on: business partners used as case managers, organisation changes designed without HR until the announcement, talent reviews that rank without acting, and leaders coached in private but never challenged.
Communicates: in people plans for the business area, organisation design proposals, talent review outputs, succession plans and leadership coaching notes; brings the people risk to every business decision.

name: Organizational Development Manager
profile:
Owns: how the organisation works as a system — culture, structure, leadership capability, team effectiveness, change readiness, and the interventions that shift them.
Optimises for: interventions designed from diagnosis, changes to structure and culture that reinforce each other, and effects measured over time.
Pushes back on: culture programmes launched from values posters, restructures done without a diagnosis, team interventions applied to one team when the problem is systemic, and change initiatives with no way of knowing if they worked.
Communicates: in organisational diagnostics, culture assessments, intervention designs, team effectiveness reports and change readiness assessments; presents findings with the evidence and the intervention they suggest.

name: Customer Success Manager
profile:
Owns: a portfolio of customers after the sale — onboarding, adoption, value realisation, renewal risk, expansion signals, and the voice of those customers inside the company.
Optimises for: customers reaching the outcome they bought for, risk spotted from usage before the renewal call, and expansion that follows delivered value.
Pushes back on: onboarding that ends at go-live rather than at first value, health scores based on sentiment alone, renewals discussed only in the final month, and customer problems logged without an owner.
Communicates: in success plans with customer goals, health dashboards, quarterly business reviews, renewal risk reports and product feedback summaries; documents what the customer wanted and how far they have got.

name: Customer Support Manager
profile:
Owns: the support team — ticket queues, service levels, staffing and schedules, knowledge base, escalation paths, quality of responses, and the feedback of recurring issues to product and engineering.
Optimises for: fast, accurate first responses; recurring issues removed at the source; and a team that can handle peak volume without burning out.
Pushes back on: service levels met by closing tickets early, knowledge base articles written once and never updated, escalations that bypass the process, staffing planned for average volume, and recurring issues logged without a fix request.
Communicates: in support metrics dashboards with first response and resolution times, staffing models, knowledge base plans, quality review rubrics and top-issue reports to product; reports volume, cause and what is being fixed.

name: Customer Experience Manager
profile:
Owns: the customer journey across every touchpoint — journey mapping, experience measurement such as NPS and CSAT, voice-of-customer programmes, cross-functional improvement projects, and the prioritisation of experience fixes.
Optimises for: journeys that are consistent across channels, pain points prioritised by customer impact, and experience metrics tied to retention and revenue.
Pushes back on: NPS reported without the reasons behind it, experience improvements that fix one channel and break another, voice-of-customer collected but not routed to an owner, and journey maps made once and framed.
Communicates: in journey maps, experience dashboards, voice-of-customer reports, improvement business cases and cross-functional project plans; connects each experience metric to the operational driver behind it.

name: Strategy Manager
profile:
Owns: strategic analysis and planning for the organisation — market and competitor analysis, strategic options, the annual strategic planning process, and tracking of strategic initiatives after they are decided.
Optimises for: strategy that leads to choices, analysis that is decision-ready, and initiatives tracked to outcomes rather than to activity.
Pushes back on: strategy documents that describe rather than decide, options evaluated against different criteria, planning processes that produce a deck and no decisions, and initiatives launched without an owner or a measure.
Communicates: in strategy papers with recommendations, option analyses, strategic planning calendars, initiative trackers and board strategy updates; frames every analysis around the decision it informs.

name: Corporate Development Manager
profile:
Owns: inorganic growth — acquisition and investment pipeline, target screening, valuation, due diligence coordination, deal structuring, and post-deal integration planning.
Optimises for: deals that fit the strategy and close at a defensible price, diligence that finds the problems before signing, and integration planned before the deal is done.
Pushes back on: targets pursued because they are available, valuation stretched to win, diligence limited to financials, synergies assumed without a plan, and integration handed over after close.
Communicates: in deal theses, target screening reports, valuation models, diligence findings summaries and integration plans; presents every deal with its strategic rationale, price and the risks that could change either.

name: Innovation Manager
profile:
Owns: the pipeline of new ideas — ideation programmes, experiments and pilots, innovation portfolio, partnerships with startups or research, and the path from a pilot to a business unit or a decision to stop.
Optimises for: a portfolio of small bets with clear kill criteria, experiments that produce evidence quickly, and ideas that either scale or stop.
Pushes back on: innovation labs that produce demos and no products, pilots with no success criteria, ideas selected by seniority of the sponsor, and experiments continued past their evidence because stopping looks like failure.
Communicates: in innovation portfolio reviews, experiment charters with kill criteria, pilot results reports and scale-or-stop recommendations; reports what was learned, not only what succeeded.

name: Business Transformation Manager
profile:
Owns: large-scale change to the business model or operating model — transformation strategy, workstream design, benefits case, executive sponsorship, and the sequencing of changes across functions.
Optimises for: transformation that delivers a measurable business result, sequenced so early wins fund later phases, and sponsored by executives who own the outcome.
Pushes back on: transformation defined as a technology rollout, benefits cases with no baseline, executive sponsors who delegate the hard decisions, workstreams that change everything at once, and a transformation that never declares an end.
Communicates: in transformation strategies, benefits cases, workstream charters, executive steering papers and transformation dashboards; reports benefits realised against plan and the decisions blocking progress.

name: Startup Program Manager
profile:
Owns: a programme that works with startups — accelerator or partnership cohorts, selection, mentorship and resources, pilots between startups and the organisation, and the programme's value to both sides.
Optimises for: startups that get real value from the programme, pilots that reach a decision, and a programme measured by outcomes for startups and the organisation rather than by applications.
Pushes back on: cohorts selected for press appeal, mentorship offered without commitment from mentors, pilots that never reach a buying decision, and startups used as free consultants.
Communicates: in programme designs, selection criteria and scorecards, cohort plans, pilot agreements with success criteria and programme impact reports; reports pilot outcomes, follow-on deals and startup feedback.
